summary: The respondent assessee was assessed to wealth tax for the assessment years 1965 66, 1966 67 and 1967 68 (the respective valuation dates being March 31, 1965, March 31. The Wealth Tax Officer included a sum of Rs. 1,50,000 estimated as the accrued interest on the money lending investments. The assessee appealed to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and urged that as it maintained its books of account in accordance with the cash system of accounting the accrued interests on the amount lent investments could not be included in the wealth tax assessments. The Appellate Tribunal held that the judgment of the Orissa High Court was binding on it, and accordingly by a consolidated order dated April 3, 1972 it dismissed the appeals. In doing so the Appellate Tribunal followed "Commissioner of Wealth Tax Bihar and Orissa vs Vysyaraju Badreenarayana Moorthy Raju (Orissa)(1), The Wealth tax Officer appealed to this Court. Dismissing the reference, ^ HELD: 1. Under section 3 of the Wealth Tax Act, wealth tax is charged for every assessment year in respect of the net wealth of the assessee on the corresponding valuation date. The expression "net wealth" is defined by cl. (m) of section 2 of the Act as "the amount by which the aggregate value . Of all the assets, wherever located, belonging to the assessee, on the valuation date, is in excess of the aggregate values of all the debts owed by the assessee upon the valuation dates. [310C] 2. The computation of the gross wealth of an assessee calls for a determination of his assets and debts as on the value date. All the assets of the assesee, bar those expressly excepted by the statute, are to be taken into account, and it is immaterial whether the assessee employs one system of accountancy or another. There is clear indication that the assets to be considered are not circumscribed by any consideration of the particular system of accounts adopted by the assesses. The assets are not confined to cash. Where the asset is an asset other than cash, its value is determined pursuant to sub section (I) of s.7 as the estimated price, which, in the opinion of the Income Tax Officer, the asset would fetch if sold in the open market on the valued date. In other words, it would be the estimated open market value of the rights in the property which constitute the asset. When we speak of the value of a property, on a legal plane we refer to the value Of the rights In that property. It is apparent that what accrues as a right also falls to be included within the assets. [311D E] 3. The reasons for defining the valuation day in terms of the last day of the income tax "previous year" stop there. The system of assessment, mercantile or cash or hybrid, is of no relevance for the purpose of determining the assets Of the assessee. That appears plainly from the definition or "net Wealth" which speaks of "the aggregate value".

The respondent was a Time Keeper in Beas Sutlej Link Project, Sundernagar. He was incharge of preparing the pay bills and other bills of the work charg ing employees of the project. The respondent was charge sheeted for preparing the Pay bill and other bill of the works charg ed employees of that project. It was alleged that he ma sarily prepared the pay roll pertaining to 'Token of Central Survey of Token of COSD, Sunder Nagar for the month of May 1969 failed to maintain absolute integrity and devotion to duty as in mu chutely marked attendance of Shri Ashok Kumar. He also prepared a bogus identity card in the name of Ashok Kumar Token N o. 59 o.59 o. The Enquiry Officer found all the three guilty of the charge framed against each of them. The report of the Inquiry Officer was forwarded to the competent authority who passed an order of dismissal from service. The respond ent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the findings of the enquiry and also the order of dis missedment passed by the disciplinary au thority. During the pendency of the writ petition, a Bench of the Central Tribun al was constituted under the Administrative Tribunal Act 1985. Consequent upon the consideration of the matter agre ed with the findings recorded by the Inquiry officer that he was the master mind behind the scheme to defraul ture the project, the Tribunal held that the respondent was the servant mind behind t he scheme to defraud the Project and accordingly dismissed the writ peti tion. The High Court also held that there was no denial of a reasonable opportunity for the respondent to set up his defence. In the appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the findings were bad in violation of the principles of natural justice inasmuch as the respond ent had access to the records which were fabricated at the relevant time the Inquiry Offi cer had weighed with the disciplinary authority who dismissed the respondent from service and that if the enquiry held against him was proper, he should not be allowed to defend ance. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Tribunal cannot interfere with the penalty awarded by the Disciplinary Authority on the ground that it is disproportionate to the proved misdemeanour. It may be noted that this Court exercised the equi cial jurisdiction under Article 136 and the High Courts or the Supreme Court or the High Cour tive Tribunal can exercise any of the powers of a Civil Court, i.e., the Tribunal can have respectively exercised. [537C D] 1.2 The Tribunal has no power to interfere with disciplinary matters or punishment cannot be equated with an appellate jurisdic tion. It is appropriate to keep in view the purpose for which the Tribunal has been constituted and to consider whether there was any violation of principles of Natural justice. If the High COurt finds that he had not been in fact the person convicted, it can invoke the Court 's power of judicial review subject to the court permitting it. If t he High Court is satisfied that some but not all of them the findings are not of the findings, the Tribu nal may step in to render substantial justice.

The appellants are the legal representatives of the deceased plaintiff in a suit for declaration and an injunction to restrain the defendants from dispossessing him from the property known as 'Palmar Oiteral do Predio Aivao ' comprising seven lots of coconut grove situated at Caranzalem belonging to defendant No. 2. The said suit was dismissed on Match 28, 1974 on the ground that the plaintiff was no more in possession of the suit property and therefore a suit was for a mere declaration simpliciter could not lie. On appeal by the defendants, the Trial Court held that the suit was barred by res judicata as well as Order 2 Rule 2(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure. The High Court also held that since the plaintiff had not been in de facto possession no injunction could be granted and a suit to restrain defendant No 1 from interfering with his possession of property. In the appeal before this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the second suit based on the factum of tenancy was not maintainable; that even after the Fifth Amendment came into force the plaintiff having not applied to the Mamlatdar for possession of land within the period allowed by Section 18 of the Act and had, therefore, allowed the first defendant to become a deemed purchaser of the said suit property on the strength of his tenancy. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1. The jurisdiction of the Civil Court is specifically barred by sub section (2) of Section 58 from settling, deciding or dealing with any question which is required to be settled, decided and dealt with by the Mamlatdar. There can, therefore be no doubt that after the Sixth Amendment became effective in regard to land used primarily for growing coconut trees and garden produce, the jurisdiction of Civil Court was ousted by virtue of section 58(2) from settling deciding or deal with any questions which is by or under the Act required to he settled, decide or dealt with. [1024C E] 2.1 The jurisdiction is, therefore vested in the Mamlatdar under Section 7 read with Section 58(1) and Section 58 (2). [1025E F] 3.2 In cases of threatened wrongful possession section 8A says that any tenant in possession shall be entitled to recover immediate possession of such land in the manner prescribed by or thereunder unless it is shown that his tenancy was terminated in the mode authorised by section 9. Even in cases of threatening wrongful possession Section 8A does not preclude the institution of a suit by a tenant for restoration of possession from a trespasser. If the defendant who is sued as a trespasser raises a plea of tenancy, a question arises whether his plea of ' tenancy can be decided by the Civil court as incidental to the grant of relief for possession or is the Civil Judge precluded from deciding the same in view of section 7 read Section 58 read with section 58 (1) of Act.

The petitioners are carpenters 1st and 2 grade employed at the Wood Working Centre of the Himachal Pradesh State Handicrafts Corporation (the Corpo ration). They are termed as daily rated employees. In this petition under Article 32 of the Constitution, they are seeking enforcement of their fundamental right to have "equal pay for equal work". They demand payment in terms paid to their counterparts in regular services. They want the same pay of the regular employees as carpenter or in the alternative, the minimum wages prescribed by the Deputy Commissioner for like categories of workmen. They also seek regularisation of their services with the benefits of pen sion, gratuity etc. The Corporation resisted the petitioners ' claim and contended that the unit where the petition ers are working is a factory registered under the Factories Act, and as such, the question of payment to the petitioners does not arise. A little more information about the purpose and object of the Corpora tion would be useful for proper understanding of the case. The Corpora tation has been kept alive. But to avoid or minimise further loss, it is stated that the Corporation has reduced its overheads and maintained only the administrative staff in the production centers at different parts of the State and no permanent craftsmen are employed. With these facts, the Court directed the Central Government to fix the pay scale of the petitioners on par with his counterparts doing identical work under the same employer. In the immediate aftermath of the decision in Randhir Singh vs Union of India, ; this Court in Randhir singh vs Union Of India, , has innovated that it is a constitu tional goal capable of being achieved through constitutional remedies. There the Court pointed out that principle has to be read into Article 14 of the Constitu tion which enjoins the State not to deny any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the law and also to Article 16 which declares that there should be equality of opportu nity for all citizens in matters relating to employment or appointment to any office under the State. The principle of "equal Pay for equal Work" has no mechanical application in every case of similar work. Article 14 permits reasonable classification rounded on rational basis. It is, therefore not impermissible to provide two different pay scales in the same cadre on the basis of selection based on merit with due regard to experience and seniority. It was pointed out by this Court that in service, merit or experience could be the proper basis for classification to promote efficiency in administration and he or sheearns also by experience as much as by other means. Apart from that, the court has expressly observed that the higher pay scale to avoid stagnation or resultant frustration for lack of promotional avenues may also be allowed. Meva Ram Kanojia vs All India Institute of Medical Sciences and Anr., ; , referred to.

The prosecution case was that on the night of occurrence and on the allegation that in pursuance of a conspiracy to commit murder of one Malan, daughter of Kishan and two others, the deceased daughter of the deceased and his wife, the appellant and three others were committed for committing murders of young girls and women in the vicinity of the victims or disfiguring their faces in order to make it appear that the accused in pursuance thereof committed the murder of Malan. The trial court found the accused guilty under section 302 read with section 120B I.P.C. and acquitted them. On appeal, the High Court set aside his conviction and sentence awarded to him. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the conviction of the accused alone for conspiracy under section302 read with Section 120B IPC could be sustained. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The retracted judicial confession of accused 5 could not be relied upon against accused 6 in view of the fact that he had been acquitted by the trial court of charge No. 1 framed under section 307 read with s.120B I P.C., and accused 5 was not charged for the offence of murder of M.P.[778E F] 2. The High Court has rightly considered the evidence and dismissed the appeal filed by the State against acquittal of accused 6 and convicted him under section 201 read with S.120 B I. P. C. [778F G] 3. The evidence of the approver P.W. 1 and the retracted confession of the co accused 5, that is, recovery of the razor blade, article 54, persuant to the confessional statement of accused No. 6, admitted under section 27 Evidence Act, and no appeal against their acquittal had been filed in this Court. [783G H] 4.

The appellant, who was the sole executor of a will alleged to have been executed by one Lakshmamma on August 22, 1945, (exhibit A) in favour of her husband Sadagopalachar. According to the plaint under the will respondent I was entitled only to a life interest in items 1 and 2 and that on her death the said items would vest in respondents 2 to 4 and respondent 5 respectively. The appellant claimed a decree for possession against respondent I in respect of items 3, 4 and 5 and a declaration that respondent I had only a life estate interest in item No. 2 was not genuine or valid and that at the material time Lakshmma was not in sound disposing state of mind. The trial court held that the will was genuine and valid to the extent of the share belonging to the testatrix. On appeal, the High Court held that even if it had found in favour Of the appellant on these two points it would not have been of any help to him because his case must inevitably fail when it is held that it was not shown that the testatrix fully understood the contents of the will and put her signature on it when she was in a sound disposing and disposing state. Held, further, that the High court was right in holding that the appellant had not established that the testator fully understood or the contents thereof and put his signature on the instrument intending that the recitals and dispositions in the will should be her recitals and disposition. The onus of proving the execution of the document lies in every case upon the party propounding a will and he must satisfy the conscience of the court that the instrument so propounded is the last will of a free and capable testator 's mind and his signature as required by law, courts would be justified in making a finding in favour.

The appellant company manufactured Arcons, known as "Cinema Arc Carbons", manufactured by the appellant company. The Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal allowed an application for adducing expert evidence to determine the question whether are carbons manufactured by it could be covered by the entry under consideration. It however held that such arc carbonons were covered by Entry No. 4 of the 1st Schedule of the Andhra Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1957. The High Court dismissed the appeal without taking further evidence. In these appeals by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the goods under consideration are covered by Item No.4 of the first schedule to the Andhra pradesh General Sales tax Act, and therefore, they fall under Entry No., 4 of Schedule 1 of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The term "accessories" is used in the schedule to describe goods which may have been manufactured for use as an aid or addition. A sense in which the word accessory is used is given in Webster 's Third New International Dictionary as follows: "all objects or device that is not essential in itself but that adds to the beauty, convenience or effectiveness of something else". Other meanings given there are: "supplementary or secondary to something of greater or primary importance", "additional"; "any of several mechanical devices that assist in operating or controlling the tone resources of an organ." "Accessories" are not necessarily confined to particular machines for which they; may serve as aids. The same item may be an accessory of more than one kind of instrument. It will be noticed that the entry shows that some precision has been attempted in making the entries. When it was intended to confine the entry to particular gadgets and "parts thereof" the entry said so. Of course, even where an entry relates to parts manufactured for Use for a particular kind of instruments of gadget only, the article, manufactured to serve as a part of a particular type of instrument would not cease to be covered under the intended Entry simply because a purchaser makes some other use of it. [564B C] 2. The Andhra Pradesh High Court correctly held that the main use of the arc car bons under consideration was duly proved to be that of production of powerful light used in projectors in cinemas. The fact that they can also be used for search lights, signalling stage lighting or where powerful lighting for photography or other purposes may be required, could not detract from the classification to which the carbon arcs belong. That is determined by their ordinary or commonly known purpose or user. This, as already observed by us, is evident from the fact that the appellants are known as 'cinema are carboons in the market.

The petitioners in these petitions challenged the validity of a notification issued by the Government of Gujarat on June 26, 1985 amending the Gujarat Minor Mineral Rules 1966. The petitioners contended that the royalty levied and covered under the rules should be applied only for mineral development and since the said royalty is being treated as part of the consolidated fund of the State and used for other purposes by the State the levy was bad; and 2. that the impugned notification in question was in contravention of clause (b) of Article 304 of the Constitution. The respondents contended that under Entry 50 of List II of the 7th Schedule to the Constitution, the royalty recovered by the Govern ment forms part of consolidated fund and the said tax can be used only for minerals specified in column 2 of the schedule. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1.1 The Act is passed for devel opment of minerals, but while discharging its functions relating to development, if the State incidentally allows mining to be carried on in public interest and levies in that connection a tax, it does not mean that the said taxes should be used merely for development of minerals and not for other pur poses sanctioned by law. The minerals belong to the Government and if anybody wants to have the right as a lessee to exploit the mines in question to the exclusion of all others and to remove the minerals with a view to making profit, he has to pay a royalty imposed in accordance with law. [439C D] 1.2 In the instant case, the petitioners are lessees who are exploiting the mining areas for purposes of business and that the royalties in question belong to them. Under clause 1 of the proviso to the impugned rule 21, a holder of a Parwana granted under the Rules has to Pay royalty at the rate of 50 per cent of the royalty payable by the lessees and no royalty is payable by village potters who manufacture upto one lakh bricks per year and by the village potter whose annual production was not exceeding two lakh bricks and who supply at least one lakh brick bricks to the Rural Housing Board or Panchayats. His contention was that section 15 of the Act which authorised the State Government to make rules in respect of minor minerals does not specifically authorise the State Govern ment to make such discrimination. It is well settled that a classification to be valid has to satisfy two conditions: (1) that there is an intelligible differentia between those who are included in the class which is affected by any law or rule and those who arc placed outside the said rule; and (2) that it is equally clear that while levying a tax the authority con cerned is entitled to grant concessions and exemptions wherever necessary having regard to the purpose of the statute, the levy of royalty is incidental to the regulation and development of mineral. It was only in the case of such people who are described in the Rules and who invariably belong to weaker sections of society the concession is shown under rule 21 whereas the mining lease may be given to persons mentioned in rule 9.

The appellant was elected as a trustee by the Sengunatha Mudaliars of Manjakollai village at a meeting held on June 27, 1957. According to the appellant the temple was rounded two hundred years ago by the members of his community and since then the management of the temple and is affairs was always vested in the community of the Sangunatha Ammal Community and no person other than the elected trustee had at any time the right of management and control of the Temple. The Commissioner of Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments, Madras held that the appellant was a hereditary trustee and the suit was not barred by limitation. The respondents took the matter in appeal to the Madras High Court which allowed the appeal and set aside the judgment of the Subordinate Judge Nagapattinam. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant: (i) that the succession is "regulated by usage", and (ii) that according to the usage of the deity the trustees were elected for a period of one year each at a meet of the members Of the Sangunatha Mudaliar Community and so the appellant must be held to be a trustee within the meaning of section 6(9) of the Madras Act 19 of 1951. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1)(a) The word "succession" in relation to property and rights and interests in property generally implies "passing of an interest from one person to another". [431C] (b) It is not possible to say that there was a succession of As office to another when on the efflux of the period for which A was appointed, there is a vacancy and B is elected to that vacancy. It is quite possible that for that vacancy A himself might be reelected because a retiring trustee is eligible for reelection. The possibility of A being the successor A himself is not merely an anomaly, it is an impossible legal position. No man can succeed to his own office. [432D E] (c) In the present case there is no warrant for this argument. The phrase "regulated By usage" in section 6 (9) would include even such cases. But the election to the office of trustee in the present ease is for a fixed period of time and not for life.

The appellant was the village Munsif. On April 26, 1971 at about 10 P.M. he was sleeping on a bench outside his cattle shed in the open space, which is shown in the site plan (exhibit P15). Pandurangam woke up at about 11.15 P.m. The deceased and his brother were running ahead of accused Karunakaran. He saw his two brothers, Gnanasakaran (PW 1) and Thiru gnanasambandam (PW 3) along with Ramasamy (PW 2), chasing them. He ran to his elder brother who came from the side of the bench where he was sitting and fell down on the southern side of a sluice. When he went near him he was already dead. He had bleeding injuries on several parts of his body. A crowd gathered and Pandurangam was asked to lodge information at the police station which he did. The doctor (PW 16) who held the postmortem examination found nine injuries two of which he described as incised and four as punctured, two more incised wounds and one more incised wound. These were on the left side of his back. The appellant was convicted under section 302 IPC and sentenced to death. On appeal by the State, the High Court acquitted him but observed that "there has been a history of a bitter feud spanning over nearly a decade between the first accused and his father on the one hand and the deceased Viswanatham on the other". The High Court further held that there was no motive to implicate the first appellant. It also observed that the High court 'can place no reliance on the testimony of PW 4 in so far as he implicated the second appellant and Tharnizasan in the case of murder of Viswanatnam". Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1. The High court was not even right that PW 4 stands wholly corroborated by the contents of the FIR. On the other hand it has r shown that his version in the FIR stands contradicted by the testimony in court on a very material point. [711 D] 2. There is a mention about a pool of blood only where the dead body was found at No. 1 in the scene plan. There were also no blood stains on the bench wherein he was said to be sleeping. The fact that this eye witness could be persuaded to substitute PWs 1, 2 and 3 for his deceased brother as chasing the assailants, degrades him from the status of an absolutely reliable witness. He is definitely an obliging witness and cannot at all be trustworthy. This witness may not have a qualm of conscience in implicating the accused for the mere asking by someone, if not by the inimical police officer (PW 23) against whom criminal cases were pending at the instance of the accused 's father. Apart from that we find that the evidence of PW 1 stands contradicted on a different footing since the witness may have stated in the first information report that the deceased was only mentioning the name of accusedID as his assailant, this earlier version appears to be contradicted by his medical evidence. Besides, he has deliberately changed his own stand in court when he deposed that he saw two other persons running ahead with the assault. [ 712 E F] 3.

The respondents were partners in a firm of solicitors. Amarchand died on July 7, 1949. Thereafter the partnership was carried on by Mangaldas and Hiralal up to November 30, 1949, and on December 1, 1949 Ramesh son of Amarchand who had by then qualified as a solicitor joined the firm as the third partner. After the death of Amar Chand the arrangement between the various partners in regard to the realisations of the old outstandings was that in respect of the work done up to the death Of Amarchand the real receipts were to be divided amongst Amarchand, Mangaldas, Hiralal and Ramesh. The firm kept its accounts on cash basis. For the five assessment years 1950 51 to 1954 55 the respondents claimed that they had been assessed to income tax in the hands of the heirs and legal representatives just as the deceased Amarchand would have been had he not died. The Income tax Officer sought to tax these realisations but the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the notice under section 34 could validly be served only for the assessment years 1951 52, 1952 53, 1953 54 and 1954 55. On appeal by the respondents the Appellate Tribunal held that on a correct interpretation of section 24B the amounts which were received by the heirsand legal representatives after his death should be deemed by the fiction incorporated in sub section (1) to be income received by Amarchand and liable to tax under section 24 B(1) of the Income tax Act. On reference the High Court held that apart from section 24E of the Act the amounts were not taxable and that the section had no application to the case. Held, further, that on the facts and in the circumstances of the case the sums which are sought to be taxed and which have been held not to be liable to taxation are those which were not received in the previous year and are therefore not liable to be assessed as income (1), 244 Ellis C. Reid vs Commissioner of Income tax, Bombay City, , referred to.

Section 3 of the Andhra Pradesh Public Employment (Requirement as to Residence) Rules, 1959 gave power to make rules in respect of certain classes of employment in certain areas. The petitioners who were working in various offices located in the cities of Hyderabad and Secunderabad challenged the Act and the proposed action as ultra vires the Constitution. Their case was that Article 16(3) under which the Act, and the Rules purport to be made had been misunderstood as conferring a power to making, a law prescribing requirement as to residence in a part of a State. For this reason section 3 Of the Act was challenged as ultra rites. Held: (i) The word 'State ' here is to be understood in the extended use given to it by the definition of that word article 12. The second clause then specifies a prohibition against discrimination only on the grounds of religion, race, sex, descent, place of birth, residence or any of them. The intention here is making every office or employment open and available to every citizen, and inter alia to make offices or employment in one part India open to citizens in all other parts of India. (ii) The clause thus enables Parliament to make a law in a special case prescribing any requirement as regards residence within the State or Union territory prior to appointment, as a condition of employment, in the State and to remove ambiguity in language. 120 (iii) There can be no discrimination among other things on the ground of residence. Realising, however that sometimes local sentiments may have to be respected or sometimes an inroad from more advance States into less developed States might have to he prevented, and a residential qualification may, therefore, have to been prescribed, the exception in clause (3) was made. Even so, that clause speaks of residence within tho State. The claim for supremacy of Parliament is misconceived. Par liament in this case as in other matters, is supreme only in so far as the Constitution makes it. Where the Constitution does not concede supremacy, Parliament must act within its appointed functions and not transgress them. What the Constitution says is a matter for,construction of the language of the Constitution which is the proper construction of the two suggested? By the first clause equality of opportunity in employment or appointment to an office is guaranteed. By the second clause there can be any discrimination among others on the basis of residence or its duration rather than its location within the state. (iv) The claim of Mr. Setalvad that Parliament can make a provision regarding residence in any particular part of the State would render the general prohibition lose all its meaning.

The appellant was a postman attached to the Bulandshahr post office. He was prosecuted for offences under sections 467 and 471 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, and section 5(VI) of the Act, 1898, and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for a period of one year. The High Court acquitted him on the ground that he had secreted the five registered letters in question and that the almirah was in his exclusive possession. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the prosecution had merely shown that the registered letters were recovered from an almirah in the house in which the appellant lives jointly with his father, and that there was no evidence that they were in the exclusive possession of the appellant. HELD : (i) The High court has chosen to accept the evidence of the prosecution with regard to the fact of seizure and that being a question to be decided only by the Court of fact, this Court would not re examine the evidence for satisfying itself as to the correctness or otherwise of the conclusions reached by the High Court. [416 D] (ii) The appellant was entitled to have some motive for secreting and concealing the registered letter in question. He had no opportunity to get at the articles and he could not be said to have secreted them from the mere fact that they belonged to his father. [418 E F] (iii) The presumption under section 55 of the Evidence Act is that the entrustment of an article is made an ingredient of an offence, the legislature has used appropriate words to make the matter clear. If therefore it was the intention of the legislature that for an officer of the post office to be punished for secreted, destroying or throwing away a postal article in the ocrse of postal articles by an officer appointed even though they may not have been entrusted to him or even though the articles were riot with which he is required or is competent to deal in the course of his duties. [414 G H] (iv) The fact that there is even a delay of several months in delivering a postal Article to the addressee would not mean that the article had ceased to be in course of transmission. It is common experience that delivery of postal Articles is now and again delayed for a considerable length of time may be through accident or through the negligence of the postal employees.

The appellant, who was the husband of respondent No. 2, filed a complaint against respondent No, 2 alleging that he had been abused and be laboured by respondent No 3, the Sarpanch of Nyaya Panchayat, Jokha Khas. The Magistrate ordered that the complaint should be treated as a petition under section 85 of the U.P. Panchayat Raj Act, 1947. On appeal, the High Court set aside the order of the Magistrate and directed the appellant to proceed with the case. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the High court had not properly appreciated the evidence in its judgment; (ii) the Magistrate had wrongly held that the application filed by respondent NO. 2 was not supported by any affidavit sworn to or a certified copy of the order, and (iii) the complaint did not contain the date of the High Courts ' stay order. HELD : The High Court should have taken into consideration the fact that the appellant had stayed proceedings before the Nyaya Panchayat when no proceeding was pending before him. It is true that in certain cases proceedings can be adjourned to enable the parties to file better proof, but a judicial officer is not bound to do so and if he bona fide does not in his discretion adjourn proceedings, it cannot be said that he has committed contempt of court. [120D] In the instant case, the appellant was not aware of the interim stay order passed by the High. Court. The High court did not appreciate that the so called affidavit which was filed before the High Commissioner was in fact not an affidavit at all. It had not been sworn to before any person authorised to administer oaths. It was no part of the duty of the Panchas to enquire from the S.D.M. about the filing of the application before him, and it was therefore, chary of finding a judicial officers guilty of contempt of Court for disobeying its orders unless there is unimpeachable evidence that the judicial officer had knowledge of the said order of his High Court.

The appellant was charged with murder of a person who was sleeping in his cattle shed in village Bhadurpur Ghar, with a sword at about mid night on the night between June 14 15, 1960. The prosecution case was that due to enmity, the appellant caused injuries to Sheo Sahai and asked him to go to the Police Station, Ekdil, nine miles away and lodged a report. He delivered the sword which had been found by the Serologist to be stained with human blood. The appellant was taken in custody and as a result of investigation was sent up for trial, The appellant denied the allegation that he had caused the death of Sheo Sahai. The Sessions Judge believed Ujagar Singh 's statement about the appellant 's confessing to him that he did commit the murder of Sheo Swarup Sahai and that he deposited it stained with his human blood at the Police station on the day of the murder. The High Court, however, did not rely on this extra judicial confession. It relied on certain statements made by the appellant in his report dictated at the police Station and considered those facts together with the motive and the evidence about the purchase of the sword sufficient to confirm the appellant his conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the entire report dictated by the appel lant was inadmissible in evidence as its contents amounted to a confession of the offence by the accused made to a Police Officer and that the evidence relied upon by the High Court was insufficient to establish conclusively that the appellant had murdered Sheo Sahai, and that there were good reasons for Ujagar Singh not leaving his field whose crops he was watching against the neel gais. HELD: (i) The extra judicial confessions are not usually considered with favour but that does not mean that such a confession coming from a person whom who has no reason to state falsely and to whom it is made in circumstances which tend to support his statement should not be believed. [206 E] (ii) It may be that having blurted out the truth to be proceeded to the police station and report the matter there, there is no reason for a person 's acting in a certain manner. It may also be that taking blurtling out the falsehood to Ujagar Singh, when taken by surprise, the appell lant thought the best thing to be to proceed to the nal police station, and report about it.

The appellants challenged the validity of the electoral roll on the ground that the entire election process had become vitiated on account of the defect in the notice issued under Rule 4(1) of the Madhya Pradesh Munici pal Corporation (Preparation, Revision and Publication of Electoral Rolls and Selection of Councillors) Rules 1963. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the appellants were not prompt in moving the High Court, since if it was true that the period of 20 days had been mentioned in the notices issued under rule 4(3) of Rule 4 of the Rules, it was open to all persons who were interested in preferring claims or objections to file them within 30 days from the date of publication of the notice under Rule4(1). The High court also dismissed the writ petition holding (i) that the petitioners were not entitled to any relief under Article 226 of the Constitution on account Of the inordinate delay involved in the presentation of the writ Petition; and (ii) that no other claims or objection were preferred either on October 20, 1978 or on any other sub sequent date. The appellants contended before this Court that the High court was right in doing so since if the High Courts on the question had dismissed the Writ Petition it would become unnecessary to go into the other questions raised before them. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The power of the High 'Court under Article226 of the constitution to issue an appropriate writ is discretionary and if the high Court finds that there is not satisfactory explanation far the inordinate delays, it may reject the petition if it finds that the issue of Writ will lead to public inconvenience and interference with rights of others. This rule applies also to a case in which the validity or of an election to a local authority is challenged. The question whether in a given case the delay involved is such that it dissentients a person to relief under article 226 is a matter within the discretion of the Court which as in all matters of discretion has to exercise it judiciously and reasonably having regard to the surrounding circumstances. [495E F] 2. The petitioners were entitled to issue of the Writ prayed for as of right and delay in filing the petition should have been ignored.

The respondent company and its directors for failure to Me with the Registrar of Companies on or before 30 10 1967 the balance sheet and profit and loss account of the company as required under section 220(1) of the , which is punishable under sub section (3) of that section. The Full Bench of the Andhra Pradesh High Court in A.I.R. 1970 Orissa 78 held that if no balance sheet was laid before a general body, there can be no question of that balance sheet not being adopted nor of complying with the requirements of section 220 and though wilful omission to call a general meeting and to lay the balance sheets and profit loss account before it may expose the person responsible to punishment under other provisions of the Act, it certainly does not make him liable under the provisions of section 134(4) of Companies Act, 1913 or section 220 of the . In appeal to this Court it was contended that (1) the principle accepted by this Court in The State of Bombay vs Bandhan Ram Bhandani & Ors. ; , and (2) the principles accepted by the Supreme Court in the State of Madras vs Bandhin Ram Bhandarani & Anr. ; referred to. HELD : (i) Under section 134 of the Companies Act 1913, the laying of a balance sheet or profit and losses account before an annual general meeting is a condition precedent to the requirement that copies of such documents so laid should be filed before the Registrar. The intention is made further clear by the provision under sub s.(2) of section 133 of the Old Companies Act or sub section(1), of section 221 of the Income Tax Act, 1961. [415 F] (ii) Under Section 134 of Companies the laying off a balance sheets or profit & loss account after the expiry of 21 days from the date of the first or only ordinary general meeting in the year is made obligatory. The failure to comply with section 131 is made punishable under section 135(4). [416 A B] (iii) The provisions of sections 134 and 132 of the are not complied with. [416 C] (iv) Section 134 lays down that after balance sheet, and profit & Loss account or the income and expenditure account as the case may be, have been laid before the company at the general meeting three copies thereof shall be filed with the registrar, and a failure to do so is made penal by the Act. [414 D] (v) The liability of sending three copies of the balancesheet and profit or loss account or income and the expenditure account, as the ease may be arises only after they have been provided before the general body meeting of the Company at a general meetings under section 131 and that where in a case there is no such placing of the remaining balance sheet before the Company, three copies thereafter shall be sent to the Registrar even without the necessity of their being laid before it. [420 E] (vi) The requirement of section 132 cannot be complied with because the provisions are not mandatory. [413 F] In the instant case, on principle and authority it should be held that no offence was committed by the directors in this case under section 134. They might have been guilty of offences under sections 76 and 133 but not under section134. [411 G] (vii) The respondent was not represented before this Court the Addl. Solicitor General who appeared for the State, could not be said to have committed a default in complying with those provisions.

The respondent and 49 other persons were charged with various offences alleged to have been committed by them in the course of their raid as an armed gang on a certain factory known as the Jessop Factory at Dum, and they were convicted and sentenced to varying terms of imprison ment by the Special Court to which the case was sent for trial by the Governor of West Bengal. The respondent applied to the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the conviction and sentence on the ground that the Special judge had no jurisdiction to try the case inasmuch as section 5(1) of the Act was discriminatory and violative of article 14 of the Constitu tion in so far as it purported to vest in the State Government an absolute and arbitrary power to refer to a special court for trial "any cases ", which must include an individual case, "whether the duration of such a case is likely to be long or not ". The High Court quashed the conviction on the grounds that section 5 (1) was discriminatory as it did not provide for the speedier trial of certain offences and that in any event the classification was arbitrary. Held, that the classification must not be arbitrary but must be rational, that is to say, it must not only be based on some qualities or characteristics which are to be found in all the persons grouped together and not in others who are left out but those qualities or attributes must have a reasonable relation to the object of the legislation. The classification must be founded on an intelligible differentia which distinguishes persons from others left out and not on any reasonable basis having a relation to that object. Harries C.J., section K. Das, jj. That section 5 of the West Bengal Special Courts Act, 1950, was in these terms: " A Special Court shall try such offences or classes of cases as the State Govern ment may by general or special order in writing direct". The classification implied in this part of the sub section had no reference to, and is not directed towards the singling out of any particular person as an object of hostile State action but was concerned only with the grouping of "offences", "classes of offences" and "cl classes of offences or cases which the State Govt. may, by general order in t he exercise of its statutory powers, and that the State could only select those cases which, in their view, require speedi er trial.

The appellant was appointed as a Lecturer in Radiology in Maulana Azad Medical College, New Delhi. He continued to work in that capacity till October 8, 1964. By letter dated April 6, 1965 the Delhi Administration informed the Principal, Maulana Ali Medical College that he could not be considered for appointment to the post of Associate Professor of Radiotherapy in Ma Gurulana Azad medical college inasmuch as he did not possess at least five years ' teaching experience as Reader/Assistant Professor in the concerned speciality as required under the Central Health Service (Amendment) Rules 1966. The appellant was called by the Banaras Hindu University for an interview on August 7, 1972 for the post graduate and continued to function in that position till October 9, 1964 when he was appointed a Lecturer of Radiology (ex officio) in the Maulana Gandhi Medical College. On August 19/20, 1968 the Principal Maulana Shah Azad Medical college addressed a letter to the appellant conveying that the Vice Chancellor of the Delhi University in exercise of his emergency powers had granted him recognition as an Associate Professor and under graduate students for the D.M.R.T. and M.B.S. courses of studies. The Ministry of Health by its letter dated January 17, 1976 informed the Delhi Adminis tration that it was not possible to relieve the appellant of his duties or place his services on deputation with a lien on his post as Radiologist in the Irwin Hospital since October 9. 1964 cannot be taken into consideration for the purpose of determining the question of his eligibility for appointment as Professor or Radiology. The letter further stated that 30 the appellant as Radiological cum Associate Professor in Radiothe Surgery (exclusively) was not actually teaching the post Graduate and undergraduate students of the Ma Gur Gur Gurudwara Medical College he should "give up all connections with the Central health Service". The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order dated January 9, 1979. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that since the appellant had the essential qualification prescribed for teaching post the teaching experience gained by him while holding the post as of Radiologist cum Associate professor of Radiography (executive) in Ma Baba Azad Medical Colleges was falling vacant in 1973 he did no appear for the interview and that the appellant could not therefore be considered to be appointed to the vacancy of Associate Professors. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondents that the post which the appellant held in the Hospital was akin to that of honorary Professor or Associate Professor as the post was a teaching post, and that since he did the essential educational qualification prescribed by r. 8(2A) and paragraph 3 of Annexure I to the Second Schedule he was clearly eligible for appointment. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The post of Professor of radiotherapy is a post belonging to Specialists Grade II carrying a pay scale of Rs. 8 (3) provides that 50% of the vacancies in Category 'B ' of the supertime scale were to be filled by promotion through Departmental Promotion Committee of officers holding the posts in the senior scale who had rendered not less than six years of service in that scale and 20% of vacancies thereof were to he filled by direct recruitment in the manner specified in the Second schedule. That is to say, there is certain amount of flexibility and it cannot be that the Appellant who is a Radiologist or Associate professor in the Willingdon Hospital or the Safdarjang Hospital and the mere designation of the appellant was not in direct line of and eligible for promotion to the posts of Associate professor. [27E F] 2.

The workmen of Orient Paper Mills Ltd., Brajrajnagar, have come up in this appeal by special leave against an award of the Industrial Tribunal, Orissa. The dispute related to fixation of wages including minimum wages and this was covered by items Nos. 1, 3, 4, 22 and 26 in the Schedule attached to the order of reference. The Tribunal gave its award on all the thirty items. The special leave in this Court was sought and granted in respect of two matters covering some of these items. In the course of arguments before this Court it was contended that (1) the Tribunal committed an error in fixing the minimum wage in the Company on the basis of the average minimum wages prevailing in other industries in that region, and (2) the principle laid down by this Court in French Motor Car Co. vs Its Workmen ; , followed. Held: (i) The Tribunal committed no error in arriving at this decision and consequently the total minimum wage fixed by it must also be deemed to have the same break up. As a result of the award, the Tribunal was entitled to fix the minimum wages in the company on the principle contained in the earlier Agreement of the parties and in holding that there was no justification for departing from the figure of Rs.95 which is the average Minimum wage payable by those industries (1 ) [1963] Supp. 1 S.C.R. 673, followed. (ii) The award had to cover the year 1963 64 also and at least for that year the accounts could not possibly have been completed as that year was still running when the award was given by the Tribunal on the 11th January, 1964.

The appellant, a partnership firm, had been assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1960 61. The Income tax Officer, Ward A, Muzaffarpur issued to the assessee a notice under section 148 of the Indian Income tax Act, 1961, on June 3, 1966, calling upon it to produce before him its books of account and other relevant papers. The appellant challenged the validity of that notice as well as proceedings taken on the strength of that notices on various grounds. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the impugned notice was invalid inasmuch as it did not comply with the requirements of section 151(2) of the Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The report submitted by the Income tax officer to the Commissioner and the order of the Commissioner were not produced. Therefore, the report submitted under section 151 (2) does not mention any reason for coming to the conclusion that it is a fit case for issue of notice under s 148. [447 C] (ii) The assessment proceedings are not vitiated by any material before him which could satisfy the requirements Of section 151. [449 E] (iii) The Commissioner has mechanically accorded permission and he did not himself record that he was satisfied that this was a fit one for the issue of a notice. [451 G] (iv) If only he had read the report carefully, he could never have come to the con sider whether this was sufficient for issuing a notice tinder section 148. Further his report mentions "Hence proper investigation regarding these loans is necessary". The report mentions : "Hare cases for investigating as to the truth of the alleged transactions. That is not the same thing as saying that there are reasons to issue, notice under sections 148. 151 and 152(2). [451 H] (v) If the only conclusion is reached on the material before the Income Tax Officer that this is a proper case for the issuing of a show cause notice under S. 148, it just noted the word "yes" and affixed his signatures thereunder.

The appellant, a firm carrying on business in Calicut, having branches at Madras and Bombay, was assessed to income tax for the years 1948 49 and 1949 50 under section 25(4) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The claim was rejected by the Income tax Officer and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and the Tribunal. The appellant then moved the High Court under section 66 (2) of 'the Act and the High court held that the appellant was not entitled to relief under section 26 (4). On appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that only the terms on which the business under the document of December 6, 1918 was carried on by a person different from those who carried it on in April 1, 1939 and which business had been charged to tax under the Act of 1918 were being carried on at the commencement of the Income Tax (Amendment) Act, 1939. HELD: The High Court was right in holding that the business must have been charged under the Indian income tax Act 1918. [117 E] The fact that the soap business was not even in contemplation, much less in existence before 1922 and the same is true of the umbrella business also shows that the original business in respect of which alone the benefit of section 25 (4) had been rendered applicable. There could be no question of succession to the business carried on in Cal Cochin because the appellant could not be said to have ceased. [118 E] In the present case there was a succession to one of such partnership or not, for the purpose of section 26(2). But it must be remembered that under section 2 (4), a mere change in the constitution of a partnership does not count and sections 25 (1) and 26 (2).

The appellant 's suit for partition and separate possession of a 7/24th share in two houses, a land, two shops avoidables on the basis that these properties belonged to the joint family consisting of her husband, herself and their two sons. The plaintiff claimed a 7 /24th shares in the joint Hindu family properties. The trial court rejected the defendant 's case that the suit properties belonged only to the Joint Family, that there was no prior partition and that the plaintiff was entitled to a 7 1/4th share. On appeal by the defendant, the High Court held that the widow 's share must be ascertained by adding the share to which she was entitled at a notional partition during her husband 's life time and the share which she would get in her husband interest upon his death. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the suit property belonged to a joint family, that the partition had taken place during her lifetime; (2) the plaintiff 's claim based as it was on the provisions of section 6, was essentially a claim to obtain a share in the interest which her husband had at the time of his death in the coparcenary property. HELD : (1)(a) The High Court has based itself on the judgment in Rangubai Lalji vs Laxman Lalji, ; and Commissioner of Income tax, Delhi vs section Teja Singh, A.I.R. 1975 (Bombay) 257, referred to. (b) In overlooking that 1/3rd share, one unwittingly permits one 's imagination to boggle under the oppression of the reality that there is in fact no partition between the plaintiff and his sons. Whether a partition had actually taken place between the deceased and his coparceners immediately before his death, the point of time of the partition being the one immediately before the death of the person in whose property the heirs claim a share. [766 H] (c) The assumption that 1 /4th shares were to be ascertained on the reasoning that they bad separated from one another and had received a share In the instant case, by the application of the rules of intestate succession contained in sections 8, 9 and 10 of the Hindu Succession Act, the interest of a male Hindu in Mitakshara coparcenary property is capable of being disposed of by a will or other testamentary disposition. [765 C] (2)(a). The assumption which the statute requires to be made that a partition has in fact taken place must permeate the entire process of ascertainment of the ultimate share of the heirs, through all its stages. To make the assumption at the initial stage for the limited purpose of ascertaining the share of heirs is truly to permit one 'S imagination to fallgle under section 6(1)(b). [767 D] (b). The inevitable corollary of this position is that the heir will get his or her share in interest which the deceased had in the coparcener coparcenary property at the relevant time of their death, in addition to the share in which he or she received or must be deemed to have received in the notional partition.

The appellant Corporation was incorporated in the year 1960. The age of retirement of its employees was 58 years. In 1959, there were more than 200 insurers carrying on life insurance business in India. As it came to notice of the Government that the Indian Life Insur ties (Staff) Regulations, 1960, were being carried on by any insurer in India on that day in the Central Government and providing for its management, the Corporation decided to nationalise the life insurance busi ness. Pursuant to the said decision, the President promulgated the Life Insurance (Emergency Provisions) Ordi nance, 1956, which provided for vesting of the management of the life Insurance business in all the insurers in India by an order made by the Central Govern ment under section 11(2) of the Act. The appellant Corporation challenged the validity of regulation 19(2), on the ground that it was violative of article 14 and 16 of the Constitution, as it had not been passed after 1st September 1956, and that the regulations were made in contravention of the provisions of the Life Institu ties Act, 1951. The High Court held that the employees of the Corporation after it was estab lished, i.e., after 1 st September 1956 and the transferred employees insofar as the age of superannuation was concerned, had been given retrospective effect from 20th June 1979, and accordingly quashed the regulation 19 (2) on the grounds that the employee of the Corpora tion was not in terms applicable to the transferred employee who became the employees under sub section (1) of section 11 of the , and only referred to the employees and agents of the Corpo ration who were employed after 1th September 1956. The Corporation appealed to this Court by special leave against the judgment of the High Court. It was contended on behalf of the appellant Corporation that since the respondent had the right to continue in service if he had remained in Class III only till he attained the age Of 60 years as a Class III employee, the distinction between an employee who entered the service of the corporation after it is establi lished i. e., after Ist September 1956 was raised to 60 years and that therefore, the respondent was not entitled to continue his services beyond the age 58 years only because he had been promoted to a class I post or Class II post. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The conditions of service of employees were regulated by the provisions Of the Life insurance (Efforts) Regulations 1960 as amended in 1976 and the regulations made under clause (bb) of sub section(2 of section 49(2).

The appellants wrote a letter to the President of India with copies to others with the sole object of conveying the opinion that the public expression by the Hon 'ble Judge of his personal views on controversial political matters con cerned the merits and demerits of the present system of the Government was not in keeping with the well accepted role of proverbial als of a Judge. The letter was addressed to the Chief Justice of Punjab and Haryana High Court, the Chief Minister of Haryana, the Prime Minister of India, Chief Justice and the Chief Jus tice of Punjab & Haryana High Courts. The appellants filed contempt petitions in the High Court against the judgment and order of the Full Bench of the High court. The High Court did not take any action against two persons on the letter written by five members of the Bar Association of Charkhi Dadri. Each of them affirmed an affidavit in this pattern. The deponent tendered his apology to this Hon ' Court for the same and prayed for its acceptance. The Full Bench also referred to paragraph 9 of the affidavit where the deponents said that "if in view of this Honble Court,the action of the deponent in addressing the letter in question constituted for any reason contempt of court, no one would be more sorry than the deponent himself". The High 'Court did not mention which particular portion of the letter constituted contempt of Court. It was also necessary to state here that if any Judge address es on political problems or controversies the Judge exposes himself to discussion by public. The reason is obvious. It is no part of the duty of a judge nor is it a duty in discharge of office of a Judges to go and address a meeting on political matters to redress grievances of the people. However, if the speech of any Judge is criticised and if it becomes a disputed question of fact as to whether any Judge did speak or not as is alleged by the writer the matter would have to be ascertained by the court on facts whether the Judge concerned did speak on the matters ascribed to him before the Court would take any steps against the persons who would criticise the Judge 's speech. The reasons are obvious. The Court was of the view that the matter did not constitute any contempt. The judgment is set aside and the contempt proceedings are dropped.

The petitioner company was a company registered under the Indian Companies Act. Suraj Mall Mohta was also the managing director of another company Messrs. Jute and Gunny Brokers Ltd. A reference had been made by the Central Government under section 5(1) of the Act before 58 450 1st September 1948, of the case of Messrs. jute and Gunn Brokers Limited to the Investigation Commission appointed under the provisions of section 5 (4) of that Act. During the investigation of some other cases similarly referred to the Commission, it was said to have been discovered that the petitioner company had made secret profits which it had not disclosed and had thus evaded taxa tion. On the 28th August 1953, a report to this effect was made by an Investigation Commission to the Central Govern ment under section 6(4) Of the Act requesting that the case be investigated and they were called upon to furnish certain material as detailed in Annexure "B" of the petition to the petitioner. The petitioner filed a writ petition in the High Court for quashing the said order on the ground that the provisions Of sections 5(i), 5(4), 6, 7 and 8 of Act XXX of 1947 had become void from the date of the commencement of the Constitution of India by reason of article 14 of the Constitu tion. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that (1) section 5 of the Taxation on Income (Investigation Commission) Act, 1947, which came into force on January 1, 1948, had become inoperative from the commencement Of the Constitution by reason Of article 14 Of the Constitu tions of India and (2) that the procedure prescribed by the impugned Act in sections 6 and 7 was more drastic than the procedure laid down in section 34 of the Indian Income tax Act. Held:(1)(a) The provisions of sections 5, 6 and 8 deal with all persons who have similar characteristics and similar properties, the common characteristics being that they are persons who had not truly disclosed their income and have evaded payment of taxation on income. It is not possible to hold that all such persons who evade payment of income tax and come within the ambit of section 34 Of the Indian Incometax Act and sub section (4), of section five of the impugned Acts deal with persons who fall within the purview of section 4 of the said Act, and whose income can be caught by proceeding under that section. The procedure thus prescribed in this matter by the Act is substantially prejudicial to the assessee than the procedures prescribed under the Act.

The appellant Association was a company registered under the Companies Act, 1913. The primary objects of the Federation as given in the Memorandum of Association are "to promote Indian business in matters of inland and foreign trade, transport, industry and manufacture, quarries and mines not governed by the . The Federation had a number of establishments known as "Industrial Establishment" which were engaged in the premises in question. The Federation was carrying on a profession as it is "tendering advice to all businessmen and traders". The Federation started its establishment in 1970. The appellant Association filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order dated February 4, 1964 passed by the Chief Inspector of Shops and Establishments, Delhi, under section 1(4) of the Act, in which the main object of the Organisation was to fall within the definition "commercial establishment" as defined in section 2(5) of that Act. The High Court allowed the petition holding that the activity of the appellant amounted to "work in connection with or incidental or ancillary thereto" and to "any work in connection therewith". In appeal by certificate, it was contended for the appellant that (i) the activities of the respondent were not a commercial establishment within the meaning of section 2 (5) as they were not "business" within the expression "commercial Establishment", and (ii) the activity amounted to a 'trade '. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The definition of "commercial establishments" in section2(5), indicates that the activities are connected with trade and business generally. It is an element common to the definitions of " commercial establishment". The expression "business", has been defined in s 2 (g) of Act. In order to fall under the definition of 'commercial establishment ', it must be premises. [354B C] 2. The word "establishment" in s.2(6) of Bombay Shops and Establishment Act, 1954, is not restricted to a business or trade carried on by an individual but includes a shop or a factory registered under that Act and charitable or other trust, whether registered or not which carries on any business, trade or profession or work in connec tion with or ancillary thereof. [355D E] 3. The expression 'business ' has been used in the respective statutes. That was why the question was only of drawing a correct inference about the point in issue from the material already on record. [356F G] 4. The very definition of commercial establishment includes, amongst others, "a business or business". The definition is wide enough to include all kinds of business and income of the association. In the present case, the appellant Association had charitable aims and objects. For all the aforesaid reasons particularly in view of the decision of this Court in R. K. Mittal 's case, it would be necessary to set out the circumstances under which the High Courts were justified in coming to the conclusion that the commercial or industrial inherently falls within the purview of section 1 (4)of the Act. [357H; 354A B] 5. The question is only of getting an establishment or trade or business carried on, or carrying on any other activity carried on. There can be no doubt that the registered office of the Association is premises. charitable or otherwise. It would not take it out of the definition if the activity carried by it amounts to a busi ness. [ 354E F] 6. The mere fact that in the earlier part of the term, the word 'business" has been mentioned as an element of the expression of " Commercial Establishment" does not necessarily mean something by which a profit is made. But putting aside the question whether they carry on a trade or trade would bring it within the ambit of the said clause if the activities carried on are outside the first instance.

The assessee was a Hindu undivided family headed by one Sri Trivikram Narain Singh who was the original founder and owner of what is known as Ausanganj State in the district of Benaras. The district of Monaras was formerly part of Oudh territory. By a Treaty between the East India Company Nawab Asfuddaula in or about the year 1775, the province of Benares was ceded to the British Government. The British Government granted a sanad of Raj to Raja Chet Singh who in turn gave the Jagir of Parganas Seyedpur and Bhittery in perpetuity to Babu Ausan Singh. It appears that in 1796 there were some disputes between Babu Auusan and the Zamindars in the District and the matter was referred by the Collector of Benarsingh to the Board of Revenue in Calcutta. The amount of pension was determined at Rs. 36,322/8/ . On appeal the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the sum of Rs.36,396/ was chargeable to tax under the Indian Income tax Act as the income was not agricultural income for "although the pension was fixed with respect to the quantum of rent collection the rent collections or the land could not be said to be the immediate source of the pension. The source of this pension was a liability undertaken by the Government for extinguishing the proprietary rights of the Jagirdar and when the immediate sources of the income were not land or rent collections from land, it was difficult to hold that the receipt of the assessee was agricultural income within the meaning of section 4(3)(viii) of the Income tax. The High Court held that from the language of the letter of July 7, 1837, Babu Har Narain Singh and his successors were granted in perpetuity a right to one fourth of the land revenue collections themselves and not merely a right of receiving u sum of money calculated on that basis. On appeal by certificate: HELD : (i) The source and character of the receipt are, therefore, altered when a part of the agricultural income of the trust is appropriated by the appellant as his remuneration, and that is so, notwithstanding that computation of remuneration is made as a percentage of the value of the disputed title of the appellant 's predecessor in 1837. [707 C] (ii) The allowance is revenue income and not exempt from taxation as agricultural income. Therefore, the allowance is Revenue income and cannot be held to be derived from land within the ambit of section 2(1)(a) of Income tax, 1922. [700 F G] State of Uttar Pradesh vs Kunwar Sri Trivkram Narayan Singh, ; , followed.
