The Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation, the Karnataka State Transport Authority granted three out of the 14 permits to the Karnataka state Tourism Development Corporation and two permits to private operators. The State Transport Appellate Tribunal set aside the grant of the two permits in favour of the KarnatakaState Road Transport Corpora tion and instead granted three permits to other private operators and increased the number of permits granted to the Indian Tourism Development Corpora tation from one to three. The Tribunal took the view that having regard to the rule of preference enunciated by the proviso to section 63(7), the applications from the 'non preferred ' category had to be excluded as the number Of applications from applicants who were required to be given preference exceeded the number o permits to be granted, and it was on that ground that the grant was set aside. The High Court also took the same view in Sher Singh 's case. In appeal by special leave, it was contended for the Karnataka Sate Road Transport Corpo ration Corporation that the State Transport Appel late Tribunal and the High Court were wrong in distinguishing the decision of this Court in Sher Sing Singh ' 's Case and that the true position was that on a correct interpretation of the proviso, the preference became operative only if other things were equal. It was also urged that the fourth sub clause of the Proviso to section 64(7) did not offend article 14 of the Constitution. On behalf of the State it was submitted that the view taken by the High Courts and the State Road Appellate Tribunal was correct and that in the present case the true situation was that the preference contemplated by the said proviso could not be given to operators of tourist cars and travel agents, who may be expected to serve that purpose. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The Karnataka State road Transport Corporation Act, 1976 is a self contained code providing for reservation of certain percentage of stage carriage permits for stage carriages and contract carriages appears to be that except in the case of a notified route or notified area, where under section 68 F(1) the permit has to be necessarily granted to tho State Transport Undertaking, in all other cases, the claims of all eligible applicants must be considered on merits, applying the rules of preference wherever the claims are approximately equal. [1015C D] 2. The general scheme of the Act in the matter of grant of permits for Stage carriages and Contract Carriage appears to have been that except for in the ease of a specified notified route, the application of no applicant may be altogether excluded from consideration on the sole ground that another applicant is entitled to preference under one or the other provisions of the statute. The proviso to Section 47(1 H) does not say, for example, like section 68F(1), that the permit shall be granted to a State Transport undertaking.

The respondent purchased, by a registered instrument dated October 5, 1956, the business carried on by one Purushottam Raju under the name All India Trading Company. Purushottam Raju was the sole proprietor of the business and had been assessed to sales tax in respect of his turnover for the years 1948 49 and 1949 50. The assessee paid some amounts towards sales tax thus determined but there remained some arrears of sales tax i.e., Rs. 3836 4 0 for 1948 49, and Rs. 1218 1 9 for 1949 50 The Sales Tax authorities attempted to recover the arrears of tax from the respondent as the purchaser of the said business. The respondent 6 63 denied liability to pay sales tax but his contention was over ruled by the Deputy Commercial Tax Officer. The appellant then moved the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the orders of the Commercial Tax officer and the Board of Revenue. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that Rule 21 A was ultra vires of the rule making power of the State Government under section 19(1) and (2) of the Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The word 'assessment ' used in section 19 (2)(c) does not include the power of recovering tax assessed from a person other than the assessee. It follows therefore that Rule is beyond the rulemaking power of State Government either under section19(1), or section 19, (2). [665 B] Badridas Daga vs C.I.T., Bihar, ; Chatturam vs C I.T. Bihar, , Chattaram vs C., I. T. Bihar and Chattamuram vs Commissioner of Inland Revenue, A. 1. R. , referred to.

The appellant entered service in the Gondal State in 1927 as a jailor. The Gondal District Jail merged with the United States of Saurashtra. On March 6, 1953, he was suspended and at that time he was acting as Accountant at Rajkot Central Prison. On April 1, 1954, he filed a written statement on September 4, 1954 and an enquiry was held by him. He also examined himself and some witnesses. He was allowed to appear through an Advocate in the enquiry proceedings. The Enquiry Officer made a report and on or about January 7, 1955, the following notice was issued to him calling upon him to show cause why he should not be dismissed from service "To Shri Bhaishanker A. Joshi, Accountant, Rajkot Central Jail (Under suspension) Charges framed against him under this office. He pleaded that the plaintiff had not asked for copy of the report and had not been prejudiced by the non supply of the copy of his report. The trial court held that the failure on the part of the competent authority to provide the plaintiff with a copy of it amounted to denial of reasonable opportunity contemplated by article 311(2) of the Constitution. On appeal, the High Court held that there was no duty to supply a copy and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The liability to pay arrears of salary was not a liability arising out of a contract but was a liability in respect of an actionable wrong other than a breach of contract. [922 D] State of Bihar vs Abdul Majid, ; , followed. (ii)The High Court erred in holding that there had been a breach on the ground that it contravened article 311 (2) and that the liability to salary was also a liability which arose out of an enforceable contract within section 60(2)(a). [923 A] State Of Bihar vs Md. Abdul Majid ; , referred to.

The appellant was granted a lease of the coal and coal mining rights in respect of 400 bighas out of his total area. The lease deed provided that the northern boundary of the leasehold land was to be drawn between the two leaseholds. The western boundary was shown as the northern boundaries of the lease hold of Samanta. On June 15,1900, the appellant made an inquiry and came to know that the defendants had encroached upon their coal mines on the northern side and removed coal from the encroached portion and had rendered the remaining coal of the encroached portions unworkable. The Commissioner appointed by the Court tested the position of the six trijunction pillars shown in the map of lease dated November 23, 1900, and found that two of the trijram pillars were in their correct positions. On these allegations the appellant asked for the following reliefs: (a) That the intermediate boundary line between the appellants ' coal land and the defendants ' coal mining right be ascertained and fixed; (b)That a permanent injunction be issued against the defendants restraining them from encroaching upon the plaintiffs ' coal mines and removing coal therefrom. The respondents denied that they had encroached on the plaintiff ' coal lands and stated that the suit was barred by limitation. The trial court held that the defendant had encroached Upon the appellant 's coal land, that the lease deed was not a valid document and that the boundary could more satisfactorily be fixed with reference to the plans annexed to the subsequent lease deeds executed in favour of the successors in interest of the appellant and the respondents. On appeal the High Court accepted all the findings of the trial court and dismissed the appeal. Held: (i) The finding of the courts below that the disputed extent of land was part of the holding of the respondents, is vitiated by an error of law by the burden of proof having been wrongly thrown on the appellant. (ii) The onus was upon the plaintiff in these suits to prove that the knowledge of his father wag within three years of the suit and that is all. If he proves this, then to succeed in the plea of limitation the defendant has to prove satisfactorily that the fact that the property was in his possession became known to the plaintiff more than three years prior to the suit. (iii) The burden of proving that the title was in the possession of the defendant within three year of the date of filing of the suits, and that was all. , therefore, on the respondents it could not be held that they were guilty of any breach of contract.

The appellant, a saw mill in the State of Kerala, was in the employ of the appellant as a crosscutter. It was alleged that on June 21, 1958, Sankaran came drunk to them mill and abused them with physical violence. He was caught hold of by other workmen and taken outside. The appellant served a charge sheet on Sankaran on June 24, 1958 acting out the above facts and asked him to show cause why his services should not be terminated on account of his grave indiscipline and misconduct. Sankaran gave an explanation the same day denying the allegations of fact made against him though he admitted that he had come to the mill at the relevant time for taking his wages for that week. On July 8, 1958 Sankaran again wrote to the appellant to hold the inquiry as early as possible. On August 9, 1958 the appellant terminated the services of Sankaran under r. 18(a) of the Standing Orders without holding any departmental enquiry and the order was communicated to Sankaran. The Industrial Tribunal held that something seemed to have happened on the afternoon of June 21. 1958 but there was no evidence to prove what had actually happened. It further held that the appellant had intended to take disciplinary action against the workman but subsequently departmental proceedings were dropped and action was taken under r, 18(b) of Standing Orders. The Tribunal also pointed out that no attempt was made before it to defend the action taken under rule 18 (a) by proving the alleged misconduct. Two witnesses were produced before the tribunal in connection with the alleged offence but the Tribunal did not rely on them on the ground that the important witnesses, namely, the Engineer, the Secretary and other members of the staff whose evidence would have been of more value had not been produced and no explanation had been given why they were not produced. The tribunal therefore held that on the facts it could not come to its conclusion that Sankaran had come drunk to the Mill and abused or attempted to assault either the Engineer or the Secretary or the other officers. In appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The Industrial Court has the right to inquire into the causes that might have led to termination of service even under a rule like 18(A). The employer could defend the actions under r . 18(c) by leading evidence before the Tribunal to show that there was in fact misconduct and therefore the action was bona fide and was not colourable exercise of the power under that rule. (ii) Even if the inquiry was not held by the appellant and action taken thereunder, it is now well settled that the employer could dismiss the action under r ' 18(d).

The appellants were the owners of a theatre. The receivers granted a lease of the theatre on certain terms and conditions to two persons, Raval and Faraqui. By an agreement dated November 27, 1954, between Raval and Garaquii on the one hand and Messrs. Filmistan Distributors (India) Private Ltd., hereinafter called "Filmistan" instituted suit No. 149 of 1960 in the Court of Small Causes Ahmedabad against Raval and two other persons claiming a declaration that it was entitled pursuant to the agreement dated December 1, 1960, to exhibit motion pictures in the theatre. By order dated December 31, 1960 the suit was disposed of as compromised. It was inter alia agreed that Raval and Earaqua were bound and liable to allow Filmistans to exercise their "exhibition rights" in the Theatre; that Raval, their servants and agents were not to have any right to exhibit any picture in contravention of the terms and condi tions of the agreement. The trial Judge passed an order disallowing the objection raised by the appellants. The revision application against that order was dismissed in limine by the High Court. When the case reached hearing and the evidence of a representative of Filmistna was being recorded, counsel for the defendants asked in cross examination the question whether the "agreement between the plaintiff and the defendant Nos. 5 and 6 were barred on principles of res judicata" from agitating the question that the said document dated November 1, 1954 as confirmed by their letter dated January 31, 1955 and further confirmed by document dated December l, 1960 was not a lease; and that in any event the suit No 149 of 1961 was for declaration of the rights of Films to exhibit cinematograph films, in view of section 92 of the Evidence Act. The High Court dismissed the revision application. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants (i) that an enquiry into the nature of the legal relationship arising out of the document could be permitted to 'be put to the witnesses for Filmisthan; and (ii) that the consent decree in suit No, 149 of 1953 had not decided that the agreement was of the nature Of a lease. HELD : (i). The order passed by the trial court is set aside and the Trial Court is directed to proceed and dispose of the suit. [446 E] (ii). A consent decree accord ing to the decisions of this Court, does not operate as res judicata, because a consent decree is merely the record of a contract between the parties to a suit, to which is superadded the seal of the court. A matter in contest in a suit may operate as Res judicata only if there is an adjudication by the Court : the terms of section II of the Code leave no scope for a contrary view. [441 G] (iii) The expression "case" is not limited in its import to the entirety of the matter in dispute in an action. This Court observed in Major section Khanna vs Brig. F. J. Dillon, [1893] 1 K.B.D. 426, that the expression " case" is a word of comprehensive import and includes a civil proceeding and is not restricted by anything contained in section 115 of the Civil Procedure Code to the extent to which the Court, viz., the trial Court in the instant case, proposed to go into that question and allow the whole question, that was closed once for all by consent decree of December 1.

The respondent, a pilot Officer was granted a permanent commission in the Indian Air Force and was, therefore, inval idated from I.A.F. The Government of India issued a scheme for the benefit of ex military officials. The State of Uttar Pradesh also adopted the same scheme. Under that scheme the ex military official were appointed on contract basis for a fixed term which could be extended from time to time subject to the suitability of the official concerned but not beyond 58 years of age. Pursuant to the said scheme the respondent was appointed as Secretary in the District Soldiers Board in the district of Unnao in the State of U.P. The terms and conditions contained in the said order included the above term relating to the period of appointment and on his accepting the terms and condi tion he was appointed to the post till 30th August, 1985 and it was again extended upto 31st March, 1983 by an order dated 1st June, 1983. Again the term was extended upto 30th of August,1985 by an Order dated 1 6 1983. The respondent was required to furnish his acceptance of the terms & conditions contained therein includ ing the above terms relating to period of appoint ment and on accepting the term and conditions he was appoint ed as Secretary. The order was to be effective from the date of receipt of termination order and no charges were men tioned therein against the 1st respondent. The Respondent aggrieved by the said orders filed a Writ Petition before the High Court contending that he was entitled to salary upto the period he was enti tled to remain in service, i.e., 30th September, 1985 unless there was a further extension. But on 29.3.1985 the service of the 1 st respondent was terminated by the issue of a notice and payment of one month 's salary. The High Court allowed the Writ Petition holding that the termination order could not be sustained and the Writ petition was liable to be allowed. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the interim order entitled him to be reinstated in service irrespective of the fact whether the Governor had extended the period beyond 30th 885 of August 1985. Allowing the Appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High court has while setting aside the order of termination by its order dated 24.3 1988 directed that the respondent be treated as a person regularly appointed in Government service entitled to con tinue till he completed the age of 58 years. Even the order passed on Review on 26.7.1988 does not make out that the Respondent had put forward at that stage such a case.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 Indian Penal Code and sentenced to suffer imprisonment for life. The High Court reversed the finding of acquittal. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) An order of acquittal can be set aside for "substantial and compelling reasons" only and Courts used to launch on a search to discover those "substantial or compelling reasons". [367B] Sanwat Singh & Ors. vs State of U.P., ; , referred to. (2) The discrepancies in regard to which of them woke up first, where was the lantern and which of the neighbours came first to the scene on hearing their cries. The Sessions Judge allowed himself to be assailed by airy and fanciful doubts. [367E F] San wat Singh vs State Of Rajasthan, ; , followed. (3) An injury of the nature received by the deceased could have been caused in the manner suggested by the prosecution that is, when the deceased was lying on her right side. It is obvious that he must have been upset by the persistent refusal of the brother and mother of the deceased to send her with him to his house. He probably attributed the refusal to reluctance on the part of his wife to accompany him straightaway. [368B] (4) The injuries were inflicted with great force and its direction was upward. The location of the injury was 6 cms. below the arm pit on the left side. According to the accused, the deceased received the injury when she placed herself between P. W. 1 and himself. It was obvious that the accused did not have any deep motive to kill the deceased. It could not be said that he had any deep motives to kill his wife and that his version was more probable than the version of the prosecution. [369E F; 370A] Sanchal Singh & Anr. vs The State of Rajasthan, A.I.R. 1971 S.C.

The appellant was a Judge of the Supreme Court. He was convicted for having committed an offence under section 5(1)(c) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The High Court dismissed his appeal and convicted him. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appel lant that (i) the President is given the power to appoint the Judges of the High Court as well as of the Chief Justice of the high Court by warrant under his hand and seal after consultation with the Chief justice of India, the Governor of the State and in a case of appointment of a Judge other than the Chief Jus tice, the Chief Judge of a High Court can be removed from his office by an order of the President passed after an address by each House of Parliament supported by a majority of the total membership of that House and by a minority of not less then two thirds of the members of that house present and voting, has been presented to the President in the same session for such removal on the ground of proved misbehaviour or incapacity; (ii) the power under clause (c) is the President and it is in this manner that section 6(1) (c), which specifically enjoins that no court shall take cognizance of an offence punishable under section 161(or section 165 of the Indian Penal Code, or under sub section (2) or sub section 3A) of section 5 of this Act, alleged to have been committed by a public servant, except with the previous sanction, (a) in the case of any other person, of the authority competent to remove him from his Office; and (b) in case of a person who is employed in connection with the affairs of the Union and is not removable from his offices save by or with the sanction of the Central Government. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The power to punish a High court Judge, if one may so describe it, is to be found only in article 2 read with Article 124(4) and (5) of Article 124 of the Constitution. [835C] 2.1 In the case, the President has not been given the sole power or the exclusive power to remove a Judge either of the, Supreme Court or of theHigh Court from his place in order to enable that authority to grant sanction for prosecution of the Judge under the provisions of section 6 of the Act and this can be done only if it is read as a part of the scheme under which the public servant is required to furnish particulars of his assets with reference to which such an opinion can be formed and there is no vertical superior with legal authority enabling obtaining of information from the concerned Judge. [889E] 2:2 The President, therefore, being the authority Competent to appoint and to remove Judge, of course in accordance with the procedure envisaged in Article 124, clauses (4) & (5), placed before the President, a Judge by warrant, under his hands and seal, after consultationwith such of the Judges. [879E F] 2 :3 The power of appointment and removal of a judge other than those of the highest Court is not contemplated by section 6, but only for the purpose of deciding whether the offence under clause(e) of possession of disproportionate assets which the Public servant cannot satisfactorily account is made out prima facie. [869C] 4:1. The President has no power or authority to remove any Judge either from his residence or from his post except with a previous sanction.

The appellant was a member of a Scheduled Caste. Abhoy Pada Saha and Sudhir Kumar Mondal were the former was declared elected. The respondent challenged the validity of the order of the High Court rejecting his prayer to be declared elected, on various grounds. At the hearing of the petition by the Election Tribunal, however, he challenged the election only on the ground that Abhiman Pada was a Member of the Saha caste and not a member thereof. The Election Tribunal rejected this contention and dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The appellant was not a Sunri by caste and had not been proved to belong to the smaller caste group of Sahas. He must be held to belong lo the Scheduled Caste specified in item 40. [390 E] (ii) The Tribunal was wrong in considering the Sahas as an independent caste. [391 C] (iii) The expression "excluding" denoted that the Saha ' contemplated would, but for this word had come within the Sunri caste. It is legitimate to think that when a statute says that a thing is to be excluded from another, both things are of the same kind; if one is a caste. the other must be a caste; it follows that when the item excluded Sahas from Sunris, since Sunri was a caste group, Saha must equally be another caste group. [392 E G] (iv) The finding that Sahas were a 'a group within the ' Sunri Caste ' is irrelevant as a test for applying item 40 unless it is shown that it indicated a smaller caste Group of Sunris. It was not necessary that such part must necessarily form a sub caste. The Tribunal, therefore, rightly held that the appellant had failed to prove that the respondent belonged to a smaller community group of ' Sahas and was thereby excluded from the Scheduled Castes specified in Item 40 for he said "these Saha families, within the fold of Sunri castes".

The appellant was the tenant of a flat on the second floor of a building called "Ganga Vihar", Marine Drive, Bombay. The tenancy was a monthly one and the rent being Rs. 215. It was alleged that the appellant wanted to go to the United Kingdom for treatment of his failing eye sight and he got into touch with the police on 1 12 1948, and in conjunction with the latter, a trap was laid for the appellant. The prosecution case was that the appel lant demanded a sum of Rs. 30,000 which was later on reduced to Rs. 29,500 as consideration for putting the complainant in vacant possession of the flat and an additional amount of Rs 2,000 for the furniture, and that the complainant agreed to pay these sums. The appellant denied any aiding and abetting the prosecution and also abetted him in the commission of the two offences. The defence was that he was in search of a partner to carry on his business during his intended absence, who was also to act as caretaker of his flat anal that it was in this connection and with this object in view that he entered into negotiations with the complain ant. The Magistrate convicted him under section 19(2) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, and sentenced him to one day 's simple imprisonment and a fine of Rs 30, 000. The wife was acquitted by the Sessions Judge but the High Court summarily dismissed his appeal on 20 2 1950. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (1) the word "relinquishment" was not a term of art and was used in the section; (2) the offence arose only on receipt of any sum or consideration as a condition of the relin quishment by a tenant of his tenancy and that in the present case there was no such relinquishment. HELD : Dismissing the appeal: (1)(a) The word "reinquishment ' does not occur in the Transfer of Property Act but it is found in many of the Tenancy Acts in various provinces where there are Sec tions which deal with the 55 424 relinquishment of their holdings by tenants in favour of the landlord by notice given to him in writing. [422 D E] (b) The words "the relinquishment of his right of tenancy of any premises" do not occur In the Transfer Of Property Act, but it was found in several of the Acts in different provinces wherethere are Secs which deal With the 55 425 relinquishment of its holdings by tenant in favour o the landlordby notice given in writing to him. The section in question, it should be further noted, does not speak of relinquishment or giving up possession,in general terms.

The appellant, a partnership firm, was a partnership concern and the workmen of the Tata Engineering Company Ltd. were members of the T minority Employees Union. The company function as a consulting organisation and a service industry, and did not manufacture any product or carry on trade. Its work force consisted of engineers and supervisors and different categories of workmen. Out of 665 employees at Bombay, the draftsmen and the administrative staff number 306. These workmen were members Of the Tata Iron & Steel Company Ltd., and they served a Charter of Demands in July 1974 on the appellant and as their demands were not accepted and conciliation proceedings proved fruitless, the State Government made a reference of the dispute under section 10(1) (d), Industrial Tribunal, Maharashtra for adjudication. The Reference was numbered I. T. No. 292 of 1975. 170 The Union filed a statement before the Tribunal claiming an upward revision of the wage scales and dearness allowance and an increase from fifteen years to twenty years in the span for earning annual increments. It was urged that the Efficiency Bar as a feature of the wages scale should be removed, and that it would not be possible for the appellant to bear the additional financial burden if the demands of the Union were accepted. The Tribunal rejected the demand of the union for dearness allowance on the basis of a slab system because that would have imposed an unacceptable burden on the company 's financial capacity and there was no reason why the existing scheme of dearness allowance should be disturbed when a substantial increase was being made in the level of the basic wage. On appeal, the Tribunal took note of the elaborate scales of wages already existing in the wage structure of the appellant, and decided to modify the existing structure of scales with flat increases in each category. But it rejected the claim of the company for dearness allowances on the ground that there would be a consequent increase in the dearness allowance or house rent allowance. The Industrial Tribunal also noted that after the salaries of the employees had been fixed in the respective scales, senior employees would have to be given some more increments in the new scales according to their completed years of service. Rs. 150/ per month and Rs. 100/ respectively and Rs., 100/ above the existing wage scales. The award was challenged by the workmen before the Industrial Tribunal which held that the existing wages were fair and reasonable on a region cum industry basis and that the increase envisaged there related to an increase in dearness allowance, it was not possible for it to bear additional financial liability if the demand demands of Union were accept. It also observed that in view of the increased burden of Rs. 50/ per mensem, the company should have fixed the dearness allowances in communion with the cost of living index and should not be a fixed amount. The High Court dismissed the appeal filed by the appellant. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the workmen that having regard to the financial capacity of the Company, the Industrial Tribunals erred in making the wage scale retrospective and, in any event, in ranging the retrospectivity back to 1st January 1976. It is urged that having due regard to its financial capacity, the appellant Tribunal erred in passing the wage rates retrospective and in any case, in increasing the retrospectivity, back to 21st January, 1976. On behalf of workmen it was submitted that the amendment results in the inclusion of a flat increase of Rs 150/ to each workman in the case of Draughtsmen and Rs 100/ and Rs, 100/ in the category of Draftsmen and of Rs,100/ to every employee in the other categories had been granted under the Industrial Disputes (Bombay) Rules, 1957. It would be noted that the Tribunal was betrayed by a curious confusion in accepting the plea of the Unions that a flat increased to the pay of each workman was intended in the original wage and, consequently, it fell into the error of amending the award.

The appellant, Sasamusa Sugar Works Ltd., and its workmen, the respondents an award had been made by an Industrial Tribunal fixing the pay of the employees at Rs. 2/2/ per day, and in pursuance thereof, the management of the appellant had entered into an agreement with the respondents that effect would be given to the wage structure prescribed by the said award. This agreement was subsequently published in Bihar Gazette as a part of the award. In spite of the Award and the agreement, the appellant paid its employees only As. / 10/ per month and that led to the present claim made by the respondents under section 15 of the Act. The respondents contended before the payment of wages authority that the refusal of the appel lant to pay to them wages at the rate awarded in substance amounted to an illegal deduction from their wages, and on that basis they asked for an order from the authority directing the appellant to pay the said prescribed wages. The appellant raised two pleas against the respondents ' claim. It was urged that section 15 Of the Act was inapplicable because the rates of wages fixed by the award did not fall within the definition of wages prescribed by section 2(vi) and it also argued, that the claim of the respondents was barred by limitation. The authority rejected the appellant 's contention and held that section 2 (vi) included wages prescribed under the Industrial Tribunal Act, and so it had rejected the appellants ' contention that the applications made by them were incompetent under section15 of the , and dismissed the petition. Held: (i) The basic assumption made by Mr. Setalvad in contending that section2(vi)(a) cannot take in the wages prescribed in the award is not well founded. When an award is made and it prescribes a new wage structure, in law the old contractual wage structure becomes inoperative and its place is taken by the wage structures prescribed by it. In a sense, the latter wage structure must be deemed to be a contract between the parties, because that, in substance, is the effect of industrial adjudication. The true legal position is that when industrial disputes are decided by industrial adjudication and awards are made, the said awards supplant contractual terms in respect of matters covered by them and are substituted for them. That being so, it is difficult to accede to the argument that the wages fixed under the award cannot be treated as wages under section 2.(vi) of the Industrial Disputes Act before it was amended. (ii) The amendment has merely clarified what, in our opinion, was included in the unamended definition itself. In this connection, the South Indian Bank Ltd. vs A. R. Chacko, A.I.R. 1964 S.C. 1523, and V. B Godse, Manager, Prabha Mills Ltd., vs R. M. Naick Inspector, under the Payment of Wages Act, the Bombay High Court has interpreted section 2 of the . (iii) to include wages directed to be paid by industrial adjudica tion.

The appellant was a Sub Divisional Officer in the Public Works Department of Pepsu. He was charged with having dishonestly removed certain medicines from a hospital which he had taken to his residence and misappropriated them. The trial court convicted him under section 465, Indian Penal Code for forging the thumb impression of Parma, and under section 409 of the Indian Penal code for criminal misappropriation of Rs. 51 shown as paid to him for his wages. On appeal by the State Government the High Court held that proof that the thumb impressions in the acquittance roll were that of the appellant was sufficient to establish an offence either under section 466 or section 409, and that there having been an acquittal of the accused by the trial Magistrate, the materials on record did not justify a reversal of that verdict by the appellate court. The State appealed to this Court with certificate granted by the High Courts. It was contended for the appellant that the prosecution had failed to establish that the amount drawn by him did not reach the hands of Parama and that therefore no sanction under section 197(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure could be taken against him. Held, that the conviction of the respondent was illegal as sanction under s. 197(I) of Code of criminal procedure was necessary for prosecuting a public servant under section409 of the Government of India Act, 1935, and the absence of such sanc tion was fatal to the maintainability of the prosecution. The fact that the appellant had been acquitted by the Trial Court did not affect his conviction. The sanction under S. 197 (1) was required only in cases where the official character of the person giving the information was found to be irrelevant or extraneous. The mere fact that a public officer was involved in the very act complained of as amounting to a crime, would not make him liable for prosecution under section 196(1). Hori Ram Singh vs Emperor, A.I.R. 1948 Pat. 75, approved.

The assessee was a public limited company incorporated in the State of Cochin with branches in that State as well as in what was British India and in Travancore State. It filed its incometax return showing an income of Rs. 11,872 for the assessment year 1948 49, its accounting year being the previous calendar year. The Income tax Officer determined its assessable income to be Rs. 90 representing only the profit it made in Travancore state and under section 32(1) proviso (i) of the Travancore Act he refused a deduction of Rs 79,275 shown as loss from branches situate outside the State. The assessee 's appeal to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner was unsuccessful but the Appellate Tribunal held that the banking business of the assessee being one and indivisible for the purpose of determining the amount assessable to income tax it was entitled to deduct the losses incurred outside Travancore State from the profits accruing and arising in that state. The first respondent, Shaw Wallace & Co., was incorporated in January 1946 as a Private Limited Company to take over the business of the partnership firm of the Shaw Wallace and Co. The Head Office of the Company is at Calcutta. It has branches in Bombay, Delhi and Via Madras. The general practice of the company both at the Head Office and the Branch Offices appears to have been to retire its employees at the age of 55 though in certain cases the Company in its discretion permitted an employee to continue beyond that age. In September 1959 an agreement was entered into between the Company and its employees under which the age Of retirement was extended to 58 years subject to the employees passing a medical examination on reaching the ageof 55. The first respondent raised a dispute regarding their retirement age but the Tribunal directed that the age should be 58 but the Company may in its wisdom and with the express or implied consent of the employee concerned continue an employee after he attains that age, and it was also found that in all the awards in recent times in various concerns in Bombay region the trend had been to fix the retirement age at 60 years. The Tribunal further directed that in view of this finding of the Tribunal that in some of its earlier decisions as to the relevant trend in the Bombay region was accurate, the Tribunal took into account the fact that in the awards recent times there was a general agree ment that the date of retirement should be fixed at 60 and not at 55. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the decision of this Court in Dunzlop Rubber Co. Ltd., vs Workmen ; , relied on by the Tribunal was erroneous as the facts and circumstances disclosed by the oral and documentary evidence on record clearly showed a consistent trend in Bombay regions region to fix its retirement age. Held, further, that the Tribunal had taken considerable pains to perform this duty and it had ultimately persuaded itself to hold that no such trend was established in fact. Dunzoop Rubber Company Ltd., v The Workmen ; and Dunzyop Rubber CO. Ltd. vs Workmen, [1960] 2 S.C.R. 869, relied on.

The first respondent was the Chairman of a company which was formed in 1961 and to report to the Company Law Board inter alia "all the irregularities and contravention in respect of the provisions of or of any other law for the time being in force and the person or persons responsible for such irregularities and breach. For sub section (6) of section 10E provides that the Board shall, in section S5SCI 23(a), constitute a Company Law board and the Chairman may, with the previous approval of the Central Govern ment, delegate its functions to the Board and to control (1 ) (2)(a) of sub section 4A. (b).

The appellants were convicted under section 395 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to 5 years rigorous imprisonment. The High Court confirmed their conviction but reduced the sentence to one year 's rigorous imprisonment and fine of Rs. 100/ . In appeal to this Court it was contended that the presumption that they were dacoits ought not to have been drawn since the circumstances did not admit the drawing of such a presumption in the case, because dacoity as such is not challenged before this Court. HELD : The law advocated by Mr. Chari is not correct. If there is other evidence to connect an accused with the crime itself, however small the finding of the stolen property with him is a piece of evidence which connects him further with the offence. There is then no question of presumption. The evidence corroborating the other evidence already against him is sufficient to prove that he was concerned with the murder. [724 D E] In what circumstances the one presumption or the other may be drawn, it is not necessary to state categorically in this case. It all depends upon the circumstances under which the discovery of the fruits of crime are made with a particular accused. It has been stated on more than one occasion that if the gap of time is too large the presumption should be drawn. [624 D] In the present case, the goods stolen were not sold and were being taken back to the dealers by the cartmen. A large number of persons said to be 20 in number pelted stones at the cart men and looted the property. Immediately afterwards a number of searches were made and the goods were found with various persons who were prosecuted as offenders. The houses of 20 persons were searched and large quantities of the theft goods were recovered from them. It is impossible to think that within the short time available, these goods could have been easily disposed of to receivers of stolen property or could be placed in the custody of friends till such time as the original offenders could take them away.

The petitioners, who were manufacturers of 'Tolinner ' within the meaning of Section 5 of the , sought to challenge the vires of section 5 of t he Act on the ground that the section gave an unguided, unchanalised and arbitrary power to the State Government to include any substance as poison for the purpose of restriction to be imposed on the posses sion for sale and sale of the same. The petitioners contended that since the Act was a Central enactment it was possible of unjust and unjustified discrimination between the two manufacturers and their products, and that the impugned notification was violative of article 14 of the Constitution. Dismissing the writ petition, HELD: 1.1 The provisions of neither Section 2 nor 5 nor the impugned Notification are hit by any consti tutional limitation. [223E] 1.2 The Act is intended to regulate the importation, possession and sale and the sale of a specified poison for purposes of committing murder or mischief by poisoning cattle appears to it to be of such frequent occurrence as to render restriction on the possessi tion thereof desirable. Any substance which is used for purposes mentioned therein can definitely be declared as poison. That is what the Government have done in this case. It has become a notorious fact, which is not disputed that the Act is an Act intended to control over the traffic in poisons. Some substances which the Govern ment consider its possession for sale or sale to be regulated in the interest of health and safety of the society. This limitation is inherent in the scheme of the Act itself. Of course no comprehensive definition can be given to the word poison. Under this term it nobody can be considered to have an absolute right to carry on any trade or business. [222G H; 223A B] 1:3. The provisions contained in neither Section 3 nor 5 or the impugned notifications are hit either by any of the provisions of law. [225B C] 2.1 It is a busi ness which can be termed even as inherently dangerous to health and fire safety of society in view of the rampant misuse and sale to the poor, weak and helpless as an intoxicant. A law in such circumstances can regulate the trade. This pos session may be a dangerous one which can he termed even though inherently dangerous. [226C D] 2:2 It is not necessary that the same substance should be declared an poison for tho entire country. The notification and its application to any area would depend on the necessity to declare the substance as poisoning on the particular facts and situation prevailing in that area and the need to regu lute the possession and sell in that areas. No question of discrimination can arise in such circum stances. [227D E] 2 :3 The provisions in neither section 2 nor5 nor the notification are hit, by any con tentional limitation, and the writ peti tion is accordingly dismissed.

The assessee firm carried on business in drugs, chemicals, mercury, mercuries, mercure etc. In the assessment of income tax for the year 1952 53, relevant to the account year 1953 54, the assessee claimed a deduction of Rs. 2,68,385/ as bad debt due from the Bombay firm at the foot of its accounts. The Income tax Officer disallowed this claim on the ground that the debt did not arise in the course of the assessee 's business as Chemists and Druggists nor in the nature of a loan advanced in the ordinary course of business transactions. The Appellate Tribunal confirmed the order of the Appellate Assistant Commissioner but held that the amount was not one incurred in the business of the assesses, and that the High Court had erred in disallowing the sum claimed by the assessee. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the finding reached by the tribunal was not supported by proper discussion of the material before it and that it gave no reasons in support of its conclusions. HELD: The Tribunal was right in holding that the debts were not sent to the Bombay Firm as loans made in the normal course of its money lending business, nor in respect of any other business of assessee. [423 D] The finding with regard to the whole of the amount sought to be deducted is binding on this Court. It is true that the tribunal after catalogueing the arguments advanced at the bar has come to certain abrupt conclusions but all the tame it cannot be denied that findings reached by it are findings of fact and those findings are supported by the evidence on record. The Tribunal has found that the monies sent by the assesses to the Madras firm were not loans made, in the regular course of their money lendingbusiness, nor any interest was charged by the appellants in respect thereof.

The petitioners were the owners of certain lands which were acquired by the respondents under the provisions of Sections 17 and 19 of the Bangalore Development Act, 1976. Dismissing the Special Leave Petitions, this Court, HELD: 1. If he fails to do so and suppresses material facts, his application is liable to be dismissed. [566C] 2. In the instant case, the Special leave petitions are liable to have been rejected. [666D] 3. The Orissa Superior Judicial Service (senior branch) is a combined cadre consisting of officers holding purely judicial posts as well as posts which are essentially administrative in character. It consists of eight district and sessions judges, two additional district and Sessions Judges, secretary to Government in law department, superintendent and legal remembrance and ex officio additional law secretary to the government in law Department, member administrative tribunal and the Registrar of the Orissa High Court, in all 15 in number. All these officers are the members of the service of the State and they were before 1962 presiding over district courts or courts subordinate to them and as such were under the control of the High Court. In view of article 229 of the Constitution, the power to appoint the Registrar is exclusively that of the Chief Justice. Neither the High Courts as such nor the Governor has any hand in his appointment. The power to transfer a district judge from one post to another whether as a Judge or to one of the posts in the secretariat was in his hands. It appears that for some time past there were differences between the High court and the Government about the posting of some judicial officers. The High Court was anxious that a judicial officer occupying one of these administrative posts enumerated above should not, in the interest of judicial work, continue in that post for an unduly long time. The Government by its letter of April 2, 1965 intimated that it had no objection to adhere to the principle of three years service in an appointment at a particular station against a special post. But when it came to the question of implementing that policy, the Government was reluctant. Every time the High ' Court requested the government to release the three officers mentioned above for being posted as district and Session judges or addl. district and session judges as the case may be, the government turned down those requests on one ground or the other.

Section 15(1)(a) of the Punjab Pre emption Act, 1913 as it originally stood underwent substantial changes in 1960 and as a result thereof, a host of writ petitions 122 were filed in this Court under Article 32 of the Constitution challenging the constitutional validity of section 15 on the ground that it infringed Articles 14 and 15 of the Constitu tion. The appellant contended that since the suit land belonged to more than one co sharer and had not been sold jointly by all the co sharers, he was entitled to claim the right of pre emption under clause 'fourthly ' of section fifteen(1) (b). A similar question came up before this Court in Balwant Ram vs B. Baijnath Singh, ; , wherein a two judge Bench negatived the contention that it cannot stand after the pronouncement of this Court on the expression 'other co sharors ' in section 15(i)(b) and is therefore entitled to exercise the right conferred on him by that provision. The question was whether the suit lands belonged to different persons or not. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The object of the Legislature was to confer the right to pre empt on specified family members of the vendor or vendors in the first three clauses of section15(1). Under the Punjab Act, 1905, the corresponding provision, section 12, con ferred a right of preemption, in the case of a sale of a share of such land or properly held jointly, firstly in the lineal discendents of the vendee in male line in order of succession; secondly, in persons not included under first or second above, in order to of succession and thirdly, in other co shar ers jointly or severally. It will be noticed that priority for the exercise of the right owes statutorily fixed and even in the cases of those falling within the same class, the exercise Of right was regulated by the use of the expression, 'in order of inheritance '. The 1905 Act was repealed and replaced by the 1913 Act. Accord ing to section 15 of this Act before its amendment in 1960, in case of sale of share out of joint land or property, the right was conferred firstly on the lineal descendents who held under tenancy of the vendors or vendors; secondly in the co divideders jointly and severally. [123D E] 1.2. The expression ' other co Tra sharers ' was used in the fourth clause of the said provision to ensure that no co shar er is left out or omitted and not to deny the right teen to kinstolk cosharers covered by the preceding clauses. If the preceding clause were not erased from the statute book as unconstitu tional the kinsfolk would have exercised the right in the order of preference, for which no justification was found. [124E F] 1:3.

The respondent No. 2, a Hindu widow, had two wives. The first wife was the adopted son of the second respondent by name Anand Babu. The alienation has made an attempt to hold out that there were agreements for sale prior to the compromise for which there is no acceptable evidence. [541D E] 2. The transferee had no right created under the alleged sale deeds. Their possession is without authority of law. Ordinarily, they would have been liable to account for mesne profits. In view of this fact that there was the allegation of payment of money by the alienees. He sought to rely on certain decisions which on being referred to were found to be totally inapplicable to the facts of the case. On the other hand, it is found that a similar question arose before the Orissa High Court in the case of Bhoja Govinda Maikap & Anr. vs Janaki Dei & Ors., AIR (1980) Ori. 108 where the power of the court under Order 23, rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure in the face of an objection of one of the party to the compromised was considered.

The workmen of the appellant company, who were workers in the respondent 's industry, claimed that they were entitled to the sickness benefit for the first two days of sickness except in the case of a spell of sickness following, at an interval of not more than 15 days, the spell of illness for which sickness benefit was last paid. The workmen also felt aggrieved because by virtue of the first proviso to section 49 of the , they were not entitled to sickness benefit under the scheme of the Act. The company resisted both the cases on the ground that the benefits of sections 47 and 49 of tile Act were already admissible to workmen in Baroda with effect from December 14, 1969, and they were quite adequate, the Tribunal committed an error of law in granting the additional benefits mentioned above. Allowing the appeals by special leave, the Court ^ HELD: 1. The scheme of benefits admissible under the Act cannot be said to cover the work men 's demand for sick leave to the extent allowed by the Tribunal. [83C] 2.1 In providing for periodical payments to an insured worker in case of sickness (sickness benefit) or for medical treatment or attendance to him or the members of his family, the legislature did not intend to substitute any of these benefits for the workmen 's right to get leave on full pay on the grounds of sickness. [86D] 2:2 The Tribunal was, therefore, justified in its view that the workmen are entitled to 7 days sick leave with wages on pro duction of a medical certificate. [87E F] 3.1 The benefit of sick leave has been allowed to the workmen of those companies. It would thus appear that the appellants have not been able to show that the awards in question were illegal or unjust; or would adversely affect the economy or the indus trial peace, or lead to imbalance in the conditions of service in other industrial establishments. [888A] 3:3 The Tribunal has examined this aspect of the controversy also and given adequate reasons for allowing the benefit of 7 days Sick leave in the manner set out in the award. Such a leave could not be categorised as privilege leave as, by its very nature, it would be admissible only in the cases of actual sickness certified by a registered medical practitioner. It will thus appear from the record that even though the Act was applicable to the workers of the Precision Bearings India Ltd., Baroda, Hindustan Brown Bovari Ltd., and M.S. University Press, Baroda, the benefit could not b.e said to be adequate for it works out to about half the average wage of a workman, and even that amount is not admissible for the 1st two days ' of sickness excepting in the ease of a period of sickness certified at an intervals of not less than 15 day, the period of illness would be very much beyond the paying capacity of the industry. [898B C] 4:4 The Tribunal had examined this question also and gave adequate reasons to allow the benefit to the sick leave. [90C] 5. In the instant case, the appellants had not been unable to show any reason to disagree with the view which it has taken. As has been stated, the Act came into force in the region concerned on December 14. 1969, till then it was the practice in the glass industries to grant sick leave without wages for periods varying from 6 to 10 days. [91G] 6:5 The Tribunal could not therefore be said that to have erred in restoring the benefit which the workmen were re ceiving under the award of 1958, for it was taken away under the mistaken impression that it had been adequately replaced by the new provisions on the coming into force of the .

The appellant was detained under the , by an order of detention passed against him on the 8th June, 1955. The grounds of detention were vague and there was a sudden search by the police on the 24th August, 1954 at the appellant 's place for alleged possession of illicit liquor. which in fact was not found but it was found that the appellant was carrying on espionage on behalf of the Portuguese Government with the help of underground workers. The order of the detention was challenged on the following grounds: (1) The detaining authority acted merely at the instance of the police who were in league with the Goan National Movement and to take up professionally the cause of persons in the position of Carlos; (2) The order was mala fide as it was passed for the ulterior purpose of preventing his freedom of speech and freedom of professional activity in the sphere of Goan affairs by reason of his known views in this behalf. Held, that the right to be furnished particulars under article 22(5) to enable a proper representation being made is subject to the limitation under article 21(6), whereby disclosure of facts considered to be against public interest cannot be required. The requirement for such a communication would arise only if the detenue feeling the grounds to be vague, asks for particulars. An obligation to communicate the decision not to disclose facts considered prejudicial to public interest may well be implied in such a situation. But in the absence of any such request by the detenue, the non communication of the decision cannot be held to have hampered his constitutional right of representation and an obligation to supply cannot be implied In these circumstances it is necessary to have an idea of the grounds of preventive detention as furnished. The necessity for such communication would arises only if a detenue feeling, feeling the ground to be precise, asks whether particulars which would enable him to make a representation against the order of his detention.

The respondent was a commissioned officer in the Indian Army and was attached to the Army Ordnance Corps Training Centre, Secundrabad. It was alleged that on April 4, 1958 he committed acts of gross misconduct. The allegations were as follows: "Knowing Kumari Prakash as the daughter of a brother Officer Rao assisted her in going away from her parents protection and planning to run away with a sepoy. " He was charged with having committed acts amounting to gross misconduct under section 161 Indian Penal Code, 1860. The trial court held that the conduct of the respondent was most unbecoming of an officer and ordered administrative action to be taken under r. 14 of the Army Rules, 1954. On appeal by the Union of India, the High Court set aside the order of removal from service on the ground that r.14 of the said Army Rules was ultra vires the . The Union of lndia appealed to this Court. HELD : (i) The words "subject to the provisions of this Act" occurring in section 19 makes section 19 subject to section 45, and the Central Government has thus no power to remove a person from the service in derogation of the provisions Of section 45. But the power under section 19 is an independent power. Although section 19 uses the words "Subject to the provision of this . Act", it speaks of removal of a personfrom the service. Section 45 provides that on conviction by court martial an officer is liable to be cashiered or to suffer such less punishment as is in this Act mentioned. The appellant was a Panchayat under the C.P. & Berar Panchayat Act, 1946. On June 1, 1959, the Bombay Village Panchayat Act 1958 (Bombay Act III of 1959) came into effect in Vidharba region and by virtue of this Act the appellant was deemed to be a Panchayat. On July 14, 1961, the Panchayat passed resolution No. 2 with a view to levy octroi duty. The resolution further stated that the appellant 's appeal to the Standing Committee was rejected on September 4, 1963. Thereafter, the appellant filed an appeal before the Standing committee under section 124(5) of the Act before the Panchayat Samiti, Parseoni. The Standing Committee allowed the appeal of the Company on two grounds: (1) that it was necessary for the Panchayat to have the octroi limits fixed with the approval of the Collector before levying octroi under r. 21; and (2) that the approval was given by the Collector on January 14, 1964 relating back to April 1, 1963, and therefore the levy of octroi from April 1. 1963 was regularised. The appellant contended that r. 5 of the Fees Rules was ultra vires the powers of the rule making authority. Held:(i) The Standing committee inspected the premises of the company but in their order they have given very scanty facts, They do not say whether the tea is crushed, processed or treated chemically to convert it into a marketable commodity. (ii) Rule 5 of Rules framed under section 176(2)(XV) of C. P.C., does not require the Panchayat concerned to fix the octroi limit in the resolution passed under r .3(a). It only deals with two items, namely, (1 ) selection of the tax and the rate at which it is to be levied; and the rates at which the tax or fee to be imposed and the amount at which a tax is to levied. The inhabitants of the village would be entitled to object only to these two matters, namely (a) the tax, or fee imposed and (b) the rate. But the learned counsel for the appellant contended (i) that r . 5 was ultra rites as it had failed to fix octroi limits in accordance with law; (ii). that the Standing Committees were entitled to deal with the appeal on merits; (iii) that there was no proper publication under r, 4 of the Rules was announced by beat of drum in the village and (iv) that in any event the Collector could regularise an imposition made without the authority of law.

The appellant was convicted under section 31(1) read with section 33(1)(XIV of the , and sentenced to a fine of Rs. 250, and accused No. 1 to a penalty of Rs., 50, 736 The appellants contended that as the conciliation proceedings had continued for a period of more than 14 days as from January 17, 1952, the dismissal could not be said to be one within the words " pendency of any conciliation proceedings ". Held, that the provisions of section 12(6) Of the , did not support this contention. Section 12 contemplates that the report should be made and the proceedings closed within a fortnight and if proceedings were not closed but were carried on as they were in the present case or if the Conciliation Officer does not make his report within 14 days he may be guilty of a breach of duty but in law the proceedings do not automatically come to an end after 14 days but only terminate as provided in section 20(2)(b) Of tile Act. The provisions of sub section (6) of section 20 apply to all conciliation proceedings whether in regard to utility services or otherwise. All conciliation proceedings under this sub section shall be deemed to have concluded in the case where no settlement is reached, when the report of the Conciliation officer is received by the appropriate Government or when the reference of the Board is published under section 17, as the case may be. The conciliation proceedings therefore do not end when the complaint under section 12 (6), is made by the Conciliation Offi cer but when that report is received after the appropriate Govern ment. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the conciliation proceeding should be held to terminate when the Conciliation Officers is required under section12(6), and the termination would depend upon how soon a report is receive by the Government.

Section 28 of the Gold Control Act, 1968 confers an arbitrary and uncanalised power upon the Administrator with the result that the licensed dealer is at his mercy while seeking permission to carry on money lending or banking business on the security of any article, ornament or both in the same premises in which he carried on business as such dealer. The High Court struck down sec. 28 only on the ground that it suffers from the vice of excessive delegation of legislative power inasmuch as no criteria or guide lines have been provided by reference to which the power conferred on the Administrator to refuse permission or grant permission should be exercised and that the section confers an unguided, uncanalised and uncanalalised power without any criteria for guiding the discretion of the Administrator. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Union of India that sec.28 is part and parcel of the entire scheme of Gold Control as envisaged by the Act and the object of the enactment and the scheme affords sufficient guidance to the Administrator in the matter of exercising his discretion under that section. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The policy and the Scheme of the Act together with the necessity to ensure prevention of circumvention of the other provisions of the , afford more than sufficient guidance in the matters of exercising the power of discretion conferred on him under sec. In fact, sec. 5(1) requires that the Administrator should have regard to the policy and purposes of the .Act in making his orders. Moreover against his order under that Sec a revision lies to Central Government which implies that he will have to make judicious use of his power or discretion and any improper exercise is liable to be corrected by a higher authority. If that be so it cannot be said that unfettered or uncanalised or arbitrary power has been conferred upon the Administration under sec . Moreover, regard must be had to be the nature of the restrictions imposed by the section. [955C D] Harakchand Ratanchand Banthias vs Asst. Collector of Central Excise Poona, II Division while declaring unamended sec. 27(6) in several of its clauses referred to certain concepts which Administrator was required to take into account, and these concepts were regarded as indefinite, uncertain and vague.

The properties involved in the suit consist of agricultural lands situated in Eragudi village, Musiri Taluk, Tiruchirappalli district. According to the appellants, the said lands had been granted in Inam to the ancestor of one Ambalathadum Pachai Kandai Udayavaravar Temple by the Carnatic Rulers before the advent of British power in India. The original grant deeds were not available; but at the time of settlement of the Inams in sixties of the last century, Inam title deeds were issued in favour of the family of Pachathai Kandi Udayaravar Temple at Eravudi village. The appellants averred that the properties covered by the grant bad been granted to the original grantee burdened with the obligation of performing certain services in a Matam; and that the said properties had been alienated from time to time, and as a result of the first alienation, the appellants became entitled to them. The trial Judge examined the whole evidence and came to the conclusion that the grant of the Inam was a personal inam and that it was not a grant in favour Of the religious endowment within the meaning of the Act. On appeal by the respondents, the lower appellate Court reversed the finding of the lower Appellate Court that the existence of the temple had not been proved; but held that the appellants had proved their title to the suit properties. The High Court also took the view that the question as to whether on facts proved in this case an inference can be drawn that the previous manager or trustee had been removed from office by other persons who were acting as de facto managers of a temple de facto, has not been discussed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that article 134 B would not apply to the present case because the alienations evidenced by Exts. A 3, A 6 and A 12 show that the alienors purported to transfer the properties not as Poojaris or managers of any temple but in their individual character as owners of the said property. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The question whether a transfer effected by the manager of a Hindu religious endowment on the basis that it belongs to him and not to the religious endowments, is irrelevant for the purpose of article 134B if it is shown to have been made on the foundation that the transferor treated the properties as his own, it does appear that the two earlier Privy Council decisions in Gnanasambanda 's case lend some support to the contention. (2) The character of the representations made by the previous managers in regard to their relation with the property which is the subject matter of transfer, is relevant for the purposes of article134 B.

The appellant, a partnership firm consisting of himself and the two persons aforementioned, applied to the District Magistrate for permission to construct a modern cinema theatre in a plot of land which he proposed to take on lease in Gandhi Nagar, Jammu. The application was rejected by the District Judge as per his order dated December 29, 1977. The State Government thereupon filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the legality and validity of the orders passed by the district Magistrate and the appellate authority namely, the State Government. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the licensing authority had no power under the Act or the Rules to make such an order. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that even though the licence had originally been issued in the name of Ved Gupta, the right of operation of the licence has become the property of the firm by virtue of clauses 13 and 18 of the partnership deed and since Ved Gupta had been expelled from the partnership and had thereby ceased to be connected with the firm, he did not have the possession of the premises and he was not entitled to claim a renewal of the license. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The view taken by the learned Single Judge that the licence granted by the licensing authorities in favour of the Apsara Theatre was in favour to his individual capacity and he alone was the licensee, is erroneous. [581F] 2.1 In the light of the foregoing discussion, it is wholly unnecessary to deal with the reasons stated by the Acting Chief Justice in support of his conclusion that the impugned order was violative of principles of natural justice. The only other reason stated by him for quashing the District Magis trate 's order is that the District and Sessions Judge, Jammu had no jurisdiction or power to suspend the licence of the Theatre under any other circumstances. [583G] 2:2 It is now relevant to recall that what has happened in this case is that in a suit filed by Krishan Kumar along with 11 others, an order of temporary injunction was issued on September 23, 1980 restraining Ved Gupta from interfering in any manner with the running of the Cinema Theatre by the plaintiffs. Quite understandably, Ved Gupta on receipt of the order of permanent injunction informed the District magistrate by his letter dated September 24, 1980 that as a result of the said order, it had become impossible for him, for the time being to operate the cinema licence with effect from the date of the aforesaid letter and that he may be absolved from any liability for prosecution or any other action in law in the capacity of the licensee of the cinema in the event of any illegal act or offence being committed by others in the Cinema premises. On September 26, 1980, the Superintendent of Police, Jammu reported to the State District Magistrate that cinema exhibition in Apsa Theatre was being conducted by some persons other than the licensee and the police had challaned the licensee under section 6 of the Act. The District Magistrate was requested by the said letter that exhibition of cinematographs in the Theatre may be suspended till the final decision was rendered by the Court in favour either of the parties. It is not known how it can be said on the facts and circumstances of the case that the order passed by him directing the suspension of cinema shows in the theatre cannot be said to have visited the writ petitioners with any adverse civil consequences. They had no legal right whatever to conduct the cinema show in the cinema Theatre without a licence in contravention of the law. [584C E] 2 :3 The impugned order is not one suspending the licence issued in respect of the Dpsara Cinema by persons other then the licensee.

The respondent entered into an agreement with the appellants, of a composite character consisting of three distinct matters. The notice then went on to state that the respondent considered it necessary to issue certain directions for the "preservation of the demised premises and the goods and stock in trade etc., lying in the demised Premises" and the appellants were accordingly required not to remove the stock or raise any money on the security thereof, and to send daily reports to the Custodian. The respondent contended that he had no auth ority to issue the notice in question under section 12 of the Act. Held, that the power could be exercised only so as to override a bar imposed by any law but not the contract under which the lease is held, and this result flows according to him from the language of the non obstante clause which is limited to anything contained in any other law for the time being in force". The respondent was acting within his authority in issuing Exhibit C in so far as it concerned the lease granted in favour of the appellants. The appellant, a minor son of Raghubir Singh, was born to Raghubir Singh on 14th March, 1963 and was only 13 years of age when the ceiling proceedings were finalised by the Sub Divisional Officer on 5th May, 1976. He further held that the provisions of the old ceiling law applied to the case but the Sub division Officer had committed an error of law in determining the ceiling area under the new law i.e. the Act of 1955. The Board went on to hold that there was no provision for separate units in Chapter III B of the Act, of 1955 and the applicant Raghubir Singh and his son Surendrapal Singh constituted one unit and not two units and the case was remanded to Sub Divisional officer, Hanumangarh, for fresh determination of the calling area for Raghubir Singh. Before the Division Bench of the High Court in the writ petitions it was urged on behalf of Raghubir singh that the power of general superintendence and control over all revenue courts vested in the Board could not be exercised to the detriment of the writ petitioners much less by way of suo motu exercise of powers. The High Court held that there is no provision in Chapter II B of Rajasthan Tenancy Act, 1955 and that the Board of Revenue had appellate jurisdiction and it could not, therefore, make use of its powers of superintendence and Control and the order of the Board. Dismissing the appeal to this Court, ^ HELD: 1. Section 221 of the Rajasthan Tenancy Rules, 1955 is similar to section 107 of the Government of India Act, 1915 in the Act. [728G] 2. The power is there, and it may be exercised sparingly in extraordinary case where interest of justice requires that the board should exercise the power. Under section 107, the Government has general powers of supervision and control of all revenue Courts. It is both administrative as well judicial powers. It was open to the Board to exercise its powers on all its subordinate courts in order to regulate the functioning of subordinate courts so as to keep them within their respective spheres of jurisdiction. If the subordinate court disregards any specific provision of law and does something illegal it is open to it to the board of Revenue to interfere and set the matter right. [628G H] 3. The appeal consequently fails and is dismissed with costs.

The first respondent, a journalist, was engaged in the production or publication of the said law reports. The first respondent filed an application before the Central Government under section 12 of the , praying for the benefits conferred upon him by the Act. The Central Government rejected the claim of the first respondent and held that the law reports published by it were not newspapers within the meaning of section 2(b) of the Act and that the demand made by the Deputy Labour Commissioner to comply with the order made by him on the basis of the recommendations of the Palekar Tribunal was unsustainable. The High Court accepted the plea of the Ist respondent and declared that the Law reports published were not newspaper as defined in the Act, and that they were not the newspapers within section 2 (b) and therefore the orders made by them were invalid. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the two courts reports published in the law report were not presses but only newspaper reports which could be said to contain news so as to become newspaper. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The law reports which are being published by the Ist Respondent are newspapers and the employees employed by the first Respondent in their production or publishing of the law Reports should be extended the benefit of the orders passed by the Central Govern ment on the based on the recommendations made by Paleakar Award. [778C] 2. The expression "newspaper" is not defined in section 2 of the . The law report which are to be published by a newspaper and also comments on some of the recent decisions. Though the publication of these items by itself may not occupy a substantial part of a law report to make it a newspaper, the publication does not cease to be a newspaper within the definition of "new 'paper ' in the . [780E F] 3. The word "new" is used in the sense of "an journalist". It is not understood in the context of any particular case whether newspaper or newspaper is a newspaper. The term "newly closed" has been defined by section 2 to mean any person employed to do any work in, or in relation to, any newspaper establishment. [783G] 4. The definition of the expression "Newspaper ' is usually applied (except so far as concerns the important class of trade newspapers) to publications devoted mainly to recording current events and `periodicals ' to magazines, reviews, and journals which in so faras they are concerned with current events at all, are concerned to comment rather than to report; but newspapers merge into advertising sheets, periodicals into books and pamphlets and both into one another. [784C D] 5. The publication of items by themselves may not be a substantial portion of a newspaper report to making it a paper, but the publication is sufficient to make a law reports a newspaper which may after some time cease to he a newspaper or become a book of reference.

The appellant was a monthly tenant of the suit premises since about 2nd February, 1965. On or about 9th of February,1965 a fresh document of that date was executed and it is alleged that the licensor gave and granted his 'leave and licence ' to the licensee to use and occupy the said premises for the period of five years. Clause 2 of the agreement recites that the licensee had agreed to use the premises as above and merely for the purpose of workshop business. The period of leave and licence was to commence from 1st September, 1965 to 31st August, 1970 and it was further submitted that the appellant would be entitled to keep the keys of the said shop with him and shall be at liberty to work in the said Premises for twenty hours subject to restriction of rules and regulations imposed by the Municipal or any other local authority or authorities. The licensor had agreed that if he commits any default of any terms and conditions or fails to pay the compensation for two months or if the licensee at any time puts up false or adverse claim of tenancy or sub tenancy, the licensor shall be entitled 'to terminate the agreement and cancel and revoke the leave and license granted earlier and shall he entitled to take possession forthwith of the premises.
