It was further stipulated that the licence would be liable to be cancelled on the licensee surrendering possession of the demised premises by removing himself and his belongings on the expiry of the period for which the agreement or sooner termination or determination thereof after deducting all the dues if any for payment of compensation. The appellant filed a suit for eviction against the respondent on the ground that he was not a sub tenant as such or not, but only the subtenancy as such and therefore it was recorded that as agreed 'B.C. no preliminary issue was to be framed. The trial Judge in the instant case passed a decree in ejectment petition filed by the respondent and ordered the appellant to vacate the premises before 31st of January, 1975. Before the High Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the respondent was not the owner of the workshop and also denied that he had given the workshop to him for conducting business. It is further contended that there was sub tenancy by the Respondent in favour of the appel lant as a monthly licensee of the business with the articles and machinery belonging to the appellant and not to the respondent, and that the agreement recited that the lessor was seized and possessed of and was otherwise well entitled as the monthly tenant. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In order to get the advantage of section 15A of the Bombay Rent Act, the occupant must be in occupation of the Premises as a licensee as defined in section 5(4A) on the 1st of February 1973. If he was such a licensee, the non obstante clause of section15A(1) give him the status and protection of a tenant in spite of there being anything to the contrary in any other law or in contract. But if he was so not a licensee under a subsisting agreement on the date of its filing. It would be construed not as a mere licence but as a lease. [1060C E] 1.2 In determining whether an agreement creates between the parties, the relationship of landlord and tenant or merely that of licensor and licensee the decisive consideration is the intention of the parties. Beopar Sahayak (P) Ltd. & Ors. vs Shri Vishwa Nath & 5 others, [1987] 2 Scale 27, held inapplicable.

The respondent was a resident of the former Dholpur State and the dispute which led to the suit related to a time before the merger of the erstwhile Dholpur Union into the Matsya Union. The case of the respondent was that in 1947 certain commodities including chuni with which appeal No. 887 was concerned could only be exported from the former Rajasthan State on export permits issued by the customs department of the said State. It was also the practice in that State that when permits for export were issued, export duties had to be paid in advance though the actual export was made later. Consequently, in June 1947, the respondent applied for and was granted a permit for export of 15,000 maunds of chuni, and in connection therewith he deposited Rs. 30,000/as export duty in advance. This permit had been granted on June 28, 1947 and remained in force upto December 2, 1947. Thereafter he could not export further as his permit was not extended. He could only export 4,572 maunds and 20 seers of chiuni before December 2. On May 15, 1949, the United State of Rajasthan was formed including the Matsaya Union into which the former State of Dholpur came to be merged in 1949 never recognised the obligations of the latter State unless it chose to recognise the obligation. The respondent 's case further was that though he asked the State for refund of this advance duty, the State did not pay back the same to him. In the meantime, rapid constitutional changes took place after August 15, 1947, by which all the old laws continued till they were repealed or altered, recognised that it was liable in the same way as would have been the merging State if there was any liability on the merged State. The suits were resisted by the State of Madhya Pradesh on various grounds; but the High Court dismissed them. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The new sovereign throughout this process of integration from 1948 to 1950 must be taken to have recognised the rights of the subjects and undertaken the liability, if any, of the old States. It follows therefore that the State would be liable under article 295(2) of the Constitution to meet the liabilities of all old States which eventually were included in it subject always to this that if the new State passed any law repealing the old law which would affect the liability or even otherwise that law would prevail and the liability may disappear provided the new law is within the competence of the State legislature and does not transgress the constitutional limitations after the Constitution came into force. (ii) The expression "Government of the corresponding Indian State" used in article 295 (2) would mean only the United state of Rajasthan as it was just before January 26, 1950 but also the old old laws which came to he merged into it through the process to which we have already referred.

The appellant was a dealer in the sale and groundnut to the State Government. The State Government issued a notification under section 3 of the Madras Commercial Crops Markets Act, 1933, directing the constitution of a market committee at Virudhunagar, for the purchase and sale of commercial crops in the State of Madras and for that purpose to establish markets and make rules for their proper administration. The appellant challenged the validity of the provisions of the Act on the ground that they infringed articles 19(1)(f) and 31 of the Constitution. Held, that the provisions Of section 5 of the impugned Act were not violative of article 19(i)(f). The object of the legislation was to protect the producers of crops, particularly commercial crops, from exploitation by them and to secure better living conditions in the country. The Act did not provide for any restriction on the right to do business unless it was clearly established that the provision was too drastic and unreasonable so as to defeat the very purpose of the law. The provisions of section 5 were not only reasonable restrictions but also tend to defeat its object. The impugned provisions did not contravene article 19 (i)(g) or (g). The Act was an integrated one, and it regulates the buying and selling of commercial crop and the bulk of transactions in such markets are regulated by the provisions contained in the Act. The fact that the growers may be under some difficulties in this regard does not affect the validity or otherwise of the scheme of the statute. The object is to protect them from being exploited by unscrupulous traders, who do business in the market established and run by them. The growing of commodities for money, the business of buying and sale and the purchase of goods at fair prices are regulated and controlled by the rules made under the Act and no restrictions on the fundamental rights of the petitioners can be justified as they are not prohibited from holding their property as property. The levy of sales tax is not a trade allowance within the meaning of section 14 of the , but only an allowable deduction under that section. The contention that the appellants in C. No. 169 of 1955 were running the market as an occupation or business with high standards and that they were not prevented from doing their business for they could still be utilised for commodities other than those specified in the explanation is without substance. The definition of "trade" in section 2(f) of the Indian , includes trade allowance, which has been defined to mean a charge levied at a fixed rate for goods or goods specified in a notified area for the purpose of carrying on the business established by the Market Committee. The appellants were running a market as a dealer and were selling commodities at proper rates. The notification directing the establishment of a Market Committee was not invalid because it had no reasonable relation to the object which the legislature sought to achieve. The exemption granted under section 5(1) of Act was not only a trade allowances but also an allowable allowance under the bye law.

The appellant was convicted for murder and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed the sentence of death on appeal, but reduced it to life imprisonment. The appellant contended that the conviction should be maintained but was not accepted by the High Court. Held, that the High Courts were right in convicting the appellant under section 302 Indian Penal Code. Section 34 of the Indian Penal code is a special provision and must be read with section 149 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. It is well settled that a common intention presupposes prior concert. In a case like that, each would be individually liable for whatever injury he caused but none could be vicariously convicted for the act of any of the others; and if the prosecution cannot prove that his separate blow was a fatal one he cannot be convicted of the murder however clearly an intention to kill could be proved in his case. The circumstances showed that there was no prior meeting of minds to form a pre arranged plan. The fact that the appellant raised their axes and sticks at the assault, did not affect the conclusion of the High court that the common intention was not only to have direct proof of prior concert or proof of circumstances which necessarily lead to that inference, but also that none could he vicariously convicted of an act of murder. The evidence showed that the two accused were responsible for the death of the deceased and the appellant had no motive for the murder. There was no evidence of any prior meeting. The mere fact that there were some other persons could not be used as a motive to kill the deceased, but none would have the common object required by section 34 of Indian Penal Act.

The petitioner was a Sub Inspector of Central Public Works Department under the Ministry of Works and Housing in Government of India. He was compulsorily retired by an order dated 3.8.1976 with effect from 5.11.76 made under Rule 56(j)(i) of Fundamental Rules. The petitioner challenged that order before the High Court on the ground that he was an officiating Sub Inspector in Class II service and was compulsorily retire by exercising the power under Rule 57(j) of the Fundamental Rules, as he had not at all been retired from service on 5.10.1976. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the petitioner was an officer who was in Class I or Class II Service or post even when he held a post of either class substantively or temporarily or on officiating basis and therefore, on the date of the order he had completed the age of 54 years. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that as the petitioner had not attained the age Of 55 years by the date he had attained the maximum age of 50 years, he could have retired from serv ice with effect only from 5th November 1976 and, therefore, he cannot be deemed to have been compulsorily retired under sub clause (i). Dismissing the writ Petition, this Court, HELD: 1. Rule 56 (j) is meant to cover only those who are in a post on a regular basis, i.e., in a substantive capacity, and not on an officiating basis only. [638C] 2. The possibility of a reversion to the substantive post is not germane to the exercise of power contained in F.R. 56(1)(i). The purpose of Fundamental Rule 56 is to confer power on the appropriate authority to compulsorily retire Government servant in the public interest and the classification of Government servants into two categories covered by sub clauses (i) and (ii) has a purpose behind it. If the condi tions indicated in sub clause(i) is satisfied, namely, the Government servant is in Class 1 or Class I service or post, the benefit must substantively belong to the two classes of service or posts cannot be introduced into the scheme. The purpose is to classify Gov ernment servants into three categories and sub cl.(i) takes within its sweep those Government servants who at the relevant time are in Class 11 service or on substantive basis. [625E F] 3.

The respondents filed a suit in the Subordinate Court of Masulipatam against the appellant Corporation for recovery of Rs. 50,000 on 27th December 1960. The appellant Corporation contested the suit contending that there was no concluded contract between the deceased and the Corporation and that the insurance contracted commenced on 11th January 1961 being the date of receipt of the balance towards premium by the Corporation. It was further stated in the plaint that the office of the Divisional Manager of Masilipatam was concerned authority to settle the claim of the plaintiffs respondents and to pay the amount. The contention of the appellant was that with full knowledge of the completion of all preliminaries, the Corporation had encashed the cheques issued towards the first premium and therefore it was the case of the plaintiff respondents that the encashment of the cheques amounted in those circumstances in law to an acceptance of the proposal and the allegation about the assurance given to the deceased as alleged in the pleadings was not true nor the alleged assurance if any valid under law. It is further stated that the averments in the claim that the deceased was assured and told by the local agent and the field officer of the Corporation that the payment of the first premiums would amount to acceptance of proposal and advised the deceased to pay to the first insurance premium in full. The Trial Court held that there were no concluded contracts between the appellant and the respondent Corporation, and that as per the prospectus of Life Insurance Corporation of India the risk under the Corporation policy commenced on the date when receipt of balance towards the premium by it was only consistent with the acceptance of its proposal. It further held that the other averments in this claim that there had been a concluded contract were not established and even if such a representation was made, that did not alter the position as under the rules the payment could never amount to the acceptance or of the proposals if the proposal was not otherwise accepted. The High Court also took the view that the Corporation has not filed any evidence of any order prohibiting other officers one step below in rank, in this case, the Assistant Divisional Manager to exercise the power of Divisional Manager. In appeal by certificate, it was contended for the appellant that (1) there was a concluded and valid insurance contract between them and the Life Insurance Corpn. of India; and (2) the plea that Divisional Manager was the only competent authority to accept had not been categorically taken in the written statement filed on behalf of the respondent. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The mere receipt and retention of premium until after the death of the applicant or the mere preparation of the policy document is not acceptance. Acceptance must be signified by some act or acts agreed on by the parties or from which the law raises a presumption of acceptance. [359D E] 2.

The appellants applied for an interim injunction restraining the Bank of India from taking any steps in pursuance of a letter of credit opened in favour of M/s. V.V. D.K. Cassim & Sons, which was the subject matter of the suit. The trial court granted an interim order restraining the bank from taking proceedings in pursuance thereof and remanded the suit for trial. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the order of the High Court amounted to a judgment or a decree and the expression "final order" in section 205(1) of the Government of India Act, 1935, meant a final decision on the rights of the parties in dispute in a suit or proceeding; and that the expression 'final order ' in section 109 Code of Civil Procedure means an interlocutory order passed by the Court of the rights and obligations of the party in dispute. HELD: The order refusing to grant interim injunction did not determine the rights, and obligations, of the respondents in relation to the matter in dispute, in the suit or proceedings from which appeal has arisen, was not final within the meaning of article 133(1)(a) and (b). [707 D] In the present case the order refusing an interim relief did not finally dispose of a suit. It was not a final order within the contemplation of article133(1), because, the plaintiff 's suit as a result of the order was disposed of by the order directing the filing of a complaint under section 205 read with section 114 I.P.C. [708 G H] Mohanlal Maganlal Thakkar vs State of Gujarat, ; and Mohanlal Magan Lal Thakkar vs The King, , referred to.

Rule 174 of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 enjoins that when goods owned by one person are manufactured by another the information is required relating to the price at which the said manufacturer is selling the said goods and the person so authorised agrees to discharge all the liabili tities under the said Act and the rules made thereunder. The price at the factory gate was Rs.5, then in such a case the value would be Rs.30 being the value of the grey cloth plus the value for the job work done plus manufac turing profit and expenses. That would be the correct as sessable value. If the trader, who entrusts cotton or man made fabric to the processor for processing on job work basis, would give a declaration to the operator as to what would be his price at what he would be selling the processed goods in the market, that would be taken by the Excise authorities as the assessable value of processed fabric and excise duty would be charged to the farce on that basis provided that the declaration as to the prices at which he would he selling the processing goods in a market, would include only the price or deemed price at that which the processed fabric would leave the processor 's factory plus his profit. Rule 174 enjoins that where goods ownedby one person were manufactured by other, the information was required relating t o the price to which the aforesaid manufacturer is sell ing the said items and the persons so authorised agree to discharge any of the liablities under this Act and rules made there thereunder. In order to explain the position it is made clear by the following illustration: if the value or value of a grey cloth in the hands of the processor is Rs.20, and the value thereof of the job worked plus manufacturing profit and manufacturing expenses whatev er these may be, which will either be included in the price, at the Factory gate or deemed to be the price for the processed fabrics or fabric plus the ting profit and the manufacturing expenses but not any other subsequent profit or expenses. It is necessary to include the processor"s expenses, costs and charges plus profit, but it is not necessary to mention the trader 's profits who gets the fabrics processed processed, because those would be post manufacturing profits.

The appellant was appointed as a clerk on June 1, 1963 by the Panchayat Samiti. On March 14, 1975, he was promoted as Head Clerk on an ad hoc basis in January 1974 or the further fact that he was appointed to the post of Head Clerk. The Punjab Panchayat Samitis, Zilla Parishads (Haryana Amendment) Act, 1973 introduced extensive amendments in the Act of 1961. Section 13 of the Amending Act deleted section 33 of the Act. A plain consequence of this deletion was that the Panchayat Samitis were divested of their power to make appointments to the Panchayats. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court which dismissed it on the ground that the right to be considered for promotion is a term and condition of service, what is relevant for our purpose is not whether the appellant was entitled to be promoted but whether the Panchayat Council had the right of appointment to him to the Post of Head clerk on the date on which it purported to do so. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant 's appointment as a Head Clerk prior to his absorption in Government service had to be recognised and protected, despite the fact that such appointment was made after June 13, 1973 when the Amending Acts came into force. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1.1 The right to he considered for promotions is a terms and condition on which they were employed by the Panchayats Samiti until they are absorbed in Government Service or retire in such manner as may be prescribed. Acting in pursuance of the provision of section 14(4) of the amending Act, the Government of Haryana notified the absorption of the appellant as a Clerk though, as stated earlier he was working as a head clerk in the Loharu Panchayat Samiti and that is the post in which the Government has absorbed him. [737B C] 1.2 The appointment of the appel lant to the posts of Head Clerks being without the authority of law, the government was not bound to absorb him in the post as of a Head clerk.

The appellants filed a suit claiming that the property in dispute belonged to the Math Sauna or deity Sri Thakur Gokarneshwar Mahadeo Ji installed in the Math, and that Mahant Sadashiva Yati was in possession thereof as Mahant and Sarbarakar of the deity. The suit was contested by the first defendant, Kedar Nath Chaubey, also referred to as Uma Shankar Yati. The trial court decreed the suit but included a finding in his judgment that Sadashiv Yati had not been a regularly constituted Mahant of Math Saauna and Sarbakar of deity. Two appeals were filed in the High Court. First Appeal No. 80 of 1964 was filed by Kedar Nath Choudhury @ Uma Shankar Yadav, against the declaration that the Amauli properties were owned by Mahant Shivshankar Yati and that Sadasiv Yatati was not a regularly appointed Mahant of the Math and that the son of Mahant Shiv Shankar Yutti had inherited the property as Mahant. The High Court allowed both the appeals by its judgment and decree dated April 21, 1969. It held that the properties had been purchased by Mahant Sheo Shankar Yatti in 1921 from the personal and separate funds inherited by him from his predecessor Shivpher Yati, and the Amaul properties must, therefore, be regarded as his personal property and separate properties and they did not belong to the math or deity. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that where a nucleus of dedicated property exists, the acquisition of additional property should be attributed to the application of the nucleum and must, consequently, be treated as property belonging to the Mahant and must be regarded in his personal and independent properties and that they did no belong to Math or the deity; and that when a nuchacleus was dedicated property there could be no presumption either way. All the facts and circumstances must be taken into consideration and on a balancing of the entire evidence it has to be determined whether the property can be said to belong to Mahant or deity or is the personal property of the Mahant, the burden of proof resting on the party who makes the claim. In the present case it was difficult to conclude from the material before this Court that the total income from the properties belonging to Math and the deity left any appreciable surplus after meeting the expenditure on account of bhog, arpan deepdan daily and annual puja and the other obligations specified in the waqf deed.

The appellants who were displaced persons from West Pakistan were granted quasi permanent allotment of 24 standard acres and 15 3/4 units in the village of Raikot in Ludhiana District in 1949. Their father Sardar Nand Singh who was 42 330 found entitled to quasi permanent allotments of 40 standard acres, and 5 1/4 unit of land was given quasipermanent allotment in another village named Humbran in the same district. The two villages were, however, 25 miles or so distant from each other. Nand Singh made an application for consolidation of his lands with those of the appellants in the Village Raikot. During the pendency of this application he died and after his death, the application was continued by the appellants. This application was rejected on the ground that no land was available in the villages Raikot and that consequently their allotment had been wrongly made but referred the matter back to the Additional Custodian for decision. The Additional Custodian held that the cancellation was a result of misapprehension of the actual facts and that they were not entitled to allotment of suburban lands at all. On appeal by the appellant, the Deputy Custodian General set aside the order cancelling the allotment of land in favour of the appellant on the grounds (1) that the notification issued thereunder stood in the way of cancellation of the allotment in favour Of the appellants and (2) that r. 14(6) of the Evacuee Property Rules which came into force on July 22, 1952 stood in that way. Held, that the power conferred by section 19(1) of , is to prevail notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force. The power of the Custodian under the , to allot any property to a person or to cancel an allotment existing in favour to a displaced person rests on the fact that the property vests in him. But the consequence of the publication of the notification by the Central Government under section 12(1), with respect to any property or a class of property would be to divest the Custodian completely of his right in the property flowing from section 8 of the , and vest that property in the Central Govern ment. He would, therefore, not be competent to deal with the property in any manner in the absence of any provision in either of these two enactments permitting him to do so.

The Uttar Pradesh Public Service Commission had undertaken the recruitment to the post of Upper Zila Basic Shiksha Adhikari (Women) District Inspectress of Girls Schools/Associate Regional Inspectress of girls Schools in Uttar Pradesh Educational Service Junior Scale (Women 's Branch) The advertisement inviting applications from eligible candidates was published on May 5, 1985 and a corrigendum was published in June, 1985. The recruitment examination was in two stages written and interview/personality test. After the written examina tion was over, on the basis of the results thereof success ful candidates upto a base limit have to be called to be interviewed. On account of improper feeding into the comput er some of the candidates who had better performance in the written examination were not called and candidates securing lesser marks in the Written Examination were not only called for interview but were also finally selected. When this position was known and upon an inquiry was factually estab lished, the Public Service Com mission decided to cancel the entire recruitment examination and asked for re holding of it. The High Court upheld the action of the Public Services Commission and dismissed the writ petitions. In these appeals by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that when no defect was pointed out in regard to the written exami nation and the sole objection was confined to exclusion of a group of successful candidates in the interview from the interview, there was no justification for cancelling the written part of the recruitment examina t tion. On the other hand, it is contended on their behalf that when there was a mistake pointed out, there could be no justification to cancel it and asking for a fresh interview of all eligible candidates on the ground of improperating the written parts of the ap plic examination and the only objection was limited to exclusion by a group. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The situation could have been appropriately met by setting aside the recruitment and asking of a fresh exami cation of all ineligible candidates on that basis. [126E] 2.1 In the instant case, when no defects were pointed out regarding the written test and the main objection was restricted to exclusion, of a Group of successful candidate in the viva voce examination from the interviews, there is no justification in cancelling the re opening part of recruitment examinat tion.

The appellant brought the suit on the allegation that there was one Shiromani Nirankari Dera at Patiala, that this institution had two branches one at Landeke in Moga Tehsil and the other at Nanga Kheri in the erstwhile Patiala State, and that he, as mahant in charge of the Shiromani Dera, at Patiala had the right to manage the properties attached to the Dera. The prayer in the plaint was for recovery of possession of the Dhoera and the properties belonging to it. Som Dass, the defendant contended that the Daha at Landake was an independent Dera and that the appellant was in possession of those properties as its lawfully appointed mahant. The trial court decreed the suit. In appeal by the defendant, the decree was reversed. Against this decree, an appeal was preferred by the appellant to the High Court which held that after the death of Som Dass he was entitled to manage properties of the dhoera at Land level, that the defendant was unlawfully claiming to be the mahant of the Akera and entitled to management the properties of Dera; and that there were no grounds for setting aside the abatement. The appellant filed an appeal before the High court which held in favour of the respondent. Allowing the appeal by special leave, the Court ^ HELD: 1. The suit against Som Dass was not in his personal capacity but in his capacity as de facto mahant and that it was in a representative capacity that the appeal was sought to be continued against the defendant. [489C] 2.1 In order 22, r. 10 of the Civil Procedure Code against the person upon whom the interest had devolved, the rule that has to be applied is Order 22, rule 10 and not rule 3 or 4, whether the devolution takes place as a consequence of death or for any other reason. [490E F] 2:2. The word 'interest ' which is mentioned in this rule means interest in the property i.e., the subject matter of the suit and the interest is the interest of the person who was the party to the suit, and it was, therefore, in a Representative capacity that Som Dass would be elected as mahants against Som Das by virtue of his election as maart subsequent to the death, of Som Das. [448G] 3:3. The devolution of the interest in subject matter Of the suit took place when Shiam Dass was elected as Mahants of the Sera after the demise of Som Chand. Som Das was sued in his capacities as a person who claimed (though illegally according to the appellant) as ma mahant, and the suit against the Som Dass had been filed in his name capacity as a de facto Mahant.

The petitioners who were working as ministerial or non ministerial but not belonging to the last grade service, who had already attained the age of 55 years was to retire from service with effect from February 28, 1983. The Government of Andhra Pradesh issued a notification on October 29, 1979 stating that it had decided to reduce the age for superannuation of all Government employees, other than in the last Grade Service, from 58 to 58 years. Two notifications were issued in exercise of the power conferred by the Proviso to Article 309 read with Article 313 of the Constitution and the petitioners challenged the said order and the notifications on the ground that they violate Articles 14, 16, 21 and 300A of the constitution. The case of the petitioners was that there was no basis at all for reducing the age retirement from 58 and that the age was increased from 55 to 58 by the Government of India by a notification dated October 29. 1979 and nothing had happened since then to justify reduction of the age from 55 years. The State Government, however, rejected their contention on the view that it was arbitrary, irrational and unconnected with the object which it sought to achieve. In the writ petitions filed before this Court, the petitioners contended that the Government had acted unreasonably in not giving any previous notice to the employees which would have enabled them to arrange their affairs on the eve of retirement; that the State exchequer would have to find and pay Rs. 70 crores on one single day by way of retirement benefits, for which no budgetary provision was made; that as a result of the increase in the age, the chances of promotion of the service personnel had deteriorated resulting in widespread frustration and unemployment; that it would have resulted in grave detriment to public services of the State; and that, the decision to reduce their age of retirement from 55 was arbitrary and irrational and hence violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitu tion. Dismissing the writ petition, ^ HELD: 1. The impugned action of the Government is bad for a total non application of mind to the relevant facts and circumstances bearing on the question of the date of the report to justify a departure from it. [610 D] 2. The power conferred under H 610 the proviso to Article 311 read with article 313 is of a legislative character and is to be distinguished from an ordinary rule making power. Therefore, the amendment made to the Fundamental Rules in the exercise of power conferred on Hates by the proviso cannot be amended so as to empower the Government to alter those conditions to their prejudice and, in any event, they cannot be amend retrospectively so as not to take away rights which had accrued to them. [613 E] 3. The amendment made in February, 1983 to the Rules was beyond the powers of the rule making authority or the Legislature. No. The contention that the amendment to the Rule was beyond its powers could not be accepted because it is unscientific and unconnected With the object sought to achieved. [514 F G] 4. The fact that the decision in Moti Ram Deka had no application to the case before them since "that case did not deal with any rule relating to age of superannuation" was taken by her State Government within one month of the assumption of office by it cannot justify the conclusion that lt the decision is arbitrary because it overlooks the advance made in longevity, fixation of retirement age at 58 is also not likely to sustain the charge of arbitrariness. [625 G H] 5.

The appellants are a registered dealer in the State of Haryana. He purchased certain raw materials in the state without paying tax thereon, in view of the provision contained in section 24 of the Haryana Sales Tax Act, 1973. The assessee was not liable to pay the purchase tax on the raw materials imposed under section 9(1) of the Act. This claim has been rejected by the taxing authorities and the High Court and hence these appeals. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The purchases of raw materials by the assessees are goods on the sales of which tax is leviable under the Act though the assessees were exempt from payment of such tax by reason of section 24(1). [351G] 2. The definition also excludes from its purview "the sale proceeds of goods on which purchase tax is levied under this Act" and "the purchase value of any goods on tho sales of Which tax is payable under this act". There can be no dispute that a tax is impos ed under the statute on the goods in question when they are sold by a dealer and, indeed, the assessees would have had to pay tax on them. But let us examine what the position would be if we hold, as con tended by Shri Gupta, that the effect of the decision is that the words "or despatches the manufactured goods to a place outside the State in any manner otherwise than by way of sale in the course of inter State trade or commerce" in section 9 (1)(b) should be deemed to have been deleted from the statute. This definition includes within the definition of 'turnover ' the purchase value o f goods liable to tax under section 8 but, the goods presently in question are not laible to tax u/s 9(i) or section 6 or section 24 (3). [353C D] 3. The words "disposes of" used in clause (a)(ii) later, clause (b) also includes cases of despatches by a registered dealers of the manufactured candi dates outside the territory of India within the meaning of sub section (1)of section 5 of the Central Sales Tax. [353F] 4.

The appellants who were registered dealers under the Bombay Sales Tax Act, claimed exemption from sales tax in respect of sales of cotton sold by them to their sellers on the ground that these sales were oil FOB contracts and they continued to be the owners of the goods till the goods had crossed the customs barrier. The Sales Tax Officer rejected this claim for exemption but assessed them to sales tax on a taxable turnover including those sales. He also assessed them as to purchase tax under section 10(b) of the Bombay Act. On appeal by the sellers, the High Court held that the goods remained the sellers ' property till they had been brought and loaded on board the ship and so the sales were exempted from tax under article 286(1)(b). Held, that the words " a person " in section 8(b), must be interpreted to include a registered dealer or anybody else. The intention of the parties was that in compliance with the requirements of cl. 5(2) of Imports (Control) Order, the goods shall be the property of the licensee at the time of export would therefore mean nothing more than that the property in the goods should pass immediately before the ship goes beyond the territorial waters of the country or at the earliest when the ship leaves the port. The words " person " used in section 10 (b) must be construed to include the registered dealer and an unregistered dealer. The scheme of the Legislature clearly was that where the intention as declared has not been carried out purchase tax should be levied. To hold otherwise would be to make the declaration of the intention useless.

The respondent husband married the appellant (wife) as a second wife, way back in 1956 and a few years later had a son by her. 15 The initial warmth vanished and the jealousies of a triangular situation erupted, marring mutual affection. The respondent divorced the appellant around July 1962. A suit relating to a flat in which the husband had housed the wife resulted in a consent decree which also settled the marital disputes. For instance it recited that this respondent had transferred the suit premises, namely, a flat, in Bombay, to the appellant and also the shares of the Cooperative Housing Society which built the flat concerned. There was a reference to mehar money (Rs. 5,000/ and Rs. 180/ ) which was also stated to have been adjusted by the compromise terms. There were a clause in the compromise that the appellant declares that she had now no claim or right whatsoever against the defendant or against the estate and the properties of the defendant. The Magistrate who tried the petition for maintenance held that the respondent was a subsisting wife and awarded monthly maintenance of Rs. 300/ for the son and Rs 400/ for her subsistence taking due note of the fact that the cost of living in Bombay where the parties lived, was high, and that the Respondent had provided residential accommodation to the appel lant. This order was challenged before the Sessions Judge by the aggrieved husband who on a strange view of the law that the court under section 125 had no jurisdic tion to consider whether the applicant was a wife, dismissed the petition in allowance of the appeal. The High Court dismissed the revision petition and summarily dismissed a revision petition. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the courts below had surprisingly forgotten the plain provision in the Explanation (b) to section 125(1) of the Code which provides that "wife ' includes a woman who has been divorced by or has obtained a divorce from, her husband and has not remarried. On this foundation he urged that accepting the contention of the respondent that the wife was a divorcee his client was still entitled to an allowance. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. Every divorce otherwise eligible is entitled to the benefit of maintenance allowance and the dissolution of the marriage makes no difference to this right under the current Code. In the normal course, an order for maintenance must follow, the quantum having been determined by the learned Magistrate at the trial level. However, the husband has not examined himself to prove that he has been giving allowances to the divorced wife. His plea is his right to ignore. So the basic condition of neglect to maintain is satisfied. In a welfare oriented jurisdiction, a broader perception and appreciation of the facts and their bearing must govern the verdict not chopping little logic or tinkering with burden of proof. The next submission is that the absence of mutual consent to live separately must be made out if the hurdle of section 125 (4) is to be over come. [78G H; 79A B] 2.1 Section 127(3)(b) posits the goal and relieves; the obligor, not pro tanto but wholly. The purpose of the payment 'under any customary or personal law ' must be to obviate destitution of the divorcee and to provide her with wherewithal to maintain herself. The whole scheme of section 127(4)(b), is manifestly to recognise the substitute maintenance arrangement by lump sum payment organised by the custom of the community or the personal law of the parties. There must be a rational relation between the sum so paid and its potential as provision for maintenance. To interpret otherwise is to stultify the project. Law is dynamic and its meaning cannot he pedantic but purposeful.

The appellant, a dealer in liquor shop, had bid for Rs.11,900 (Rupees eleven thousands only) per month Dak in an auction of Beni Country liquor shop held on 27.3.88 and he as given the shop of Beni country liquor but after signing in Bandobasti Register he did not deposit dak amount. The name of Shri Raghu Nath Thakur S/o Late Gorakh Nath Village Repura, P.S. Pusa, Distt. Samastipur was placed in the black list for future under the orders passed by the Collector, Samasti. This order was passed pursuant to the order of the Collector. The letter dated 25th March, 1988 stated that no notice had been given to the appellant of the proposal of black listing the appellant. It was contended on behalf of the State Government that there was no requirement in the rule of giving any prior notice before black listing any person. In so far as the contention that there is no requirement specifically of giving a prior notice is concerned, the respondent was right. But it was an implied principle of the rule that any order having civil consequence should be passed only after following the principles of natural justice. It has to be realised that black listing every person in respect of business ventures has civil consequence for the future business of the person concerned in any event. Even if the rules do not express so, it is an elementary principle of natural Justice that parties affected by any order should have right of being heard and making representations against the order. In this view of the matter, the last portion of the order in so far it directs black listing of the appellant in respect thereof cannot be sustained in law.

The property which was the subject matter of the dispute originally formed part of an extent of land situat ed on Mount Road, Madras bearing door Nos. 2 and 3 and a building thereon. The rent for the premises was Rs. 150 per month. On 30.7.1953 all the co owners of the property (includ ing G.G.) sold the property to the United India Life Assur ance Company and the New Guardian of India Life Insurance Company Ltd. In 1956, the Life Insurance Corporation of India stepped into the shoes of these two insurance companies and became the owner of the said property. On 20.7 .65, the LIC moved two applications (being HRC Nos. 3310 and 3311 of 1965) in the court of the Rent Controller (Sri A. Varadarajan who later became a Judge of this Court) for fixation of fair rent in respect of item No. 1 as against the rent of Rs.150 p.m. fixed under the lease deed. So far as item 2 was concerned, it appears that at the time of hearing it was conceded before the Rent controller that the respondents were tenants of the entire properties covered by the lease deeds and that they had not constructed any of the premises thereupon. The Rent Controller rejected these applications on the ground that since the subject matters of the lease under exhibit P 1 was only a vacant site, the Rent Control Authority had no juris diction to fix the fair rent. On appeal, the Court of Small Causes held that the buildings on the land leased under exhibit PW 1 had also been conveyed to the LIC and that the LIC was entitled to seek fixation offair rent in regard thereof and that, therefore, the claim in the suit for arrears of rent based on Rent Controller 's order in respect thereof had to fail. The High Court held that since tho subject matter was only one vacant piece of land, it was not open to the Court to go into the question of title in view of the decision in the first set of proceedings. Allowing the appeal by special leave, the court ^ HELD: (1) In order to decide whether the denial or claim is bona fide and if he records a finding to that effect, the landlord shall be entitled to sue for eviction by having his title adjudicated upon in a civil Court but that the owner cannot have a similar right in the matter of recovery of rent which is basically a relief for which he has to approach a civil court.

The petitioner, who was a respondent in the writ petition, filed an application before the High Court for a direction to the Union of India to file his objections against the preliminary list. The High Court dismissed the application holding that the case now before it was governed by what was held by this Court in Shankariah 's case with reference to an entirely different and provisional list of Forest Officers. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. A person whose seniority is to be determined under section 115 of the Act must be given an opportunity to object to the proposed assign ment of a place to him in the seniority list. As already observed above, the petitioner had ample opportunity to do that. Hence, the principle recognised in Shankriah ' s case was not applicable to such a case. [829E F] 2. The combined final gradation list dated April 6, 1962, so far as category 6 is concerned, is ultra vires and illegal and that part of the notification alone must be quashed by grant of a writ in the nature of certiorari. [828F G] 3. A right to representation was recognised as existing at time when the list was still to be considered as not finalised presumably because some mistakes had crept in due to want of heating on two points. The petitioner had adequate opportunity to make a representation against the final gradation lists. But once he has had that opportunity, it cannot possibly be said that he should have a further opportunity against even a final seniority list.[828F] 4. If a particular decision is mala fide or arrived at on totally irrelevant and extraneous considerations ation, such a decision can be interfered with by Courts. [829G H; 829A B] 5. The Central Government had acted properly in accordance with the provisions of the . It was also held there (at p. 2106): "It is no doubt true that the Central Govern ment must have due regard to the princi ples enunciated by it in consultation with the States for the purpose of equation of posts and preparation of gradation lists." [828C D] 6. The respondents were entitled to an opportunity of making a representation with regard to two points urged by the petitioner before the final list was to be declared and published as a final list.

The petitioners in both these writ petitions are partnership firms carrying on business of import of rough diamonds and export of polished diamonds. The Import & Export Policy for the period April 1978 to March, 1991 in para 174 of the Import & Exports Policy for April 1988 to March 1979 in para 215 made provision for grant of certain import facilities to Export Houses which were registered in accordance with the provisions of the said Policy. One of the conditions was that the Export House would be eligible to Additional Licences on the basis of the export actually made in preceding three licensing years termed as 'the Base period '. The petitioners submitted application for registration as Export Houses and for grant or renewal of Export House Certificate which would have entitled them to the grant of such Additional Licence. The said applications were rejected by the authorities on the view that they had failed to diversify their export of "Other products" during the year 1977 78. The order refusing the Export Certificate was challenged by the petitioners by filing writ petitions under Article 226 of the Constitution before the Bombay High Court which dismissed the same. While the said appeal and other writ petition (filed by the Petitioners viz. Writ Petition No. 460 of 1988) were pending in the Bombay, this Court decided Civil Appeal No. 1423 of 1984, Union of India vs Rajnikant Brothers, and other connected matters by order dated April 18, 1985 wherein it was observed that there was no requirement of diversification of exports as a condition for grant/ entitlement of Export Houses in the Import Policy for 1978 79 and the Export Houses who were issued Additional Licences prior to April 1, 1988, on the ground that they have failed to carry out their export obligations during the period 1977 78 in accordance therewith. The Court further directed the authorities to grant Export House Certificates to the petitioners under the Import and Export Policy 1978 79 within three months. While construing the aforesaid direction contained in its order dated 4th April, 1985 in Rajnarayanikant Brothers case (supra) this Court has held that the grantees of the Additional Licences were not only prohibited from importing items which were excluded under the Export Policy1978 79 but also from importing item excluded under Import Policy prevailing at the time of import and that the word 'banned ' was intended to take in terms which were banned altogether as well as items which are `non canalised ' and also item which are 'canalised ' could not be ruled out and it was in this light that the Court can be said to have used the words "whether canalised or otherwise ' contained in the order dated 1st April, 1988. The High Court further held that under Import & export Policy 197879 Additional licences were to be given on the basic basis of one third of the f.o.b. value of the exports made in 1977 78 whereas under Import and export policy 1988 91 Additional Licences are to be granted on the same basis as permissible during the licensing year to which the application pertains, but the items to be allowed will be as per the Import policy in force on the date of issue of the licence. The grievance of the petitioners is confined to sub para (10) of para 218 which lays down that Additional licences issued to Export House/Trading Houses prior to 1st March, 1988 shall cease to be valid for import of items of raw materials, components and consumables covered by Appendices 3 and 5 Part A and items of non OGL capital goods (other than those covered by Appendix 1 Part A) and items available under this Policy.

The appellant is a division of McDowell & Co. Ltd., which has its factory at Visakhapatnam. It manufactures and sells fusel oil/Styrene Monomer falling under Tariff Item No. 68 of the Ist Schedule to the Act. The case of the appellant is that the said fusel Oil is a com pletely manufactured article and after completion of its manufacture, it is stored in storage tanks duly approved for this purpose. It is also the case of appellant that the aforesaid drums were sup plied by the customers for the purpose of filling the fusel oils/Stirene M accessioner. No duty of excise, therefore could be collected from the appellant on such drums which were nei ther manufactured nor purchased by the appellant. The said drums were supplied by the buyer to the customer at the appellant 's factory. The appellant had filed its price lists in respect of the same. In the said price lists, which were duly approved by the Asstt. Collector, the appellant had shown the value of fusel gas/Slyrene Moulders manufactured according to the appel lant at the rate at which those were sold in wholesale as "naked Ex Works and in bulk". According to the appellant, the manufacture of fuel oil is complete and it is the fully manufactured fusel on behalf of the appe lant. It was also the contention that on a correct and true interpretation of Section 4(4)(d)(i) of the Act, the cost of packing could be included in the assessable value only when the packing is either manufactured by the assessee or is purchased by him. The Assistant Collector included the value in the price lists. On appeal, the Collector (Appeals) held that at the time of removal, the goods were delivered from the factory in packed condition and the containers were not returnable by the buyers, there fore, the value had to be included In the assessable Value. The Tribunal, therefore, accepted the revenue 's contention and restored the order of the Asstt Collector. Collector. Aggrieved therefrom, the appell lant has come up in these appeals to this Court. On behalf of appellant it was contended that the Tribunal had failed to appreciate the admitted factual position that the fu Counsel oil/styreneMonomer manufactured by it is sold in bulk and is capable of being so sold. Hence according to him, it was not necessary for the said company to be supplied to the customers in drums in the aforesaid situation. The respondent State contended that in any event under the Act and the Rules, the duty of Excise is payable by the manufacturer on the manufactured goods. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In order to be deliverable, it has to be borne in mind that the duty is chargeable with reference to the value charged by the manufacturers, the computation being made in accordance with the terms of section 4. It has also to be bear in mind the fact that the measure of excise duty is price and not value.

The appellant was an Accountant cum Head Clerk in the Tamil Nadu Forest Training School at Vaigai Dam. He took charge of the office on 6.10.1975 and had been residing in a house opposite the training school. PW 3, the Principal of the training School issued exhibit P 2 show cause notice to the PW 1, Venkataswamy, the canteen contractor as to why his licence for running the canteen should not be cancelled. This was on the basis of a complaint made by the appellant that the food served in the canteen was substand ard. The appellant produced the currency notes. PW 6 conducted the phenolphthalein test with reference to the fingers of the appellant. The test was positive, the currency note were seized and the appellant arrested. At the trial, the prosecution witnesses supported the case. PW 1 affirmed the fact that the appellant made the demand and had also received the amount on 22.10 .1975 itself passed orders and closed the file. The Trial Court accepted the prosecution evidence, rejected the plea of the appel lant and recorded the conviction. Before this Court it was contended for the appellant: (i) that there was no independent evidence regarding the demand, the messenger who had contacted PW 1 at the behest of the accused had not been examined; (ii) that the conviction under section 161 I.P.C. and section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act is to be maintained, no separate sentence need be award ed under section161 I. P.C., and (iii) that even from the earliest opportunity that the currency Notes found in his possession was the money returned by PW 1; the cir cumstances of the case would probabalise this case of the prosecution and the presumption, if any, arising under section 4 is rebutted and the conviction cannot therefore be sustained. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The appellant had even by preponderance of probability succeeded in rebutting the presumption. [337F] State of Rajasthan vs Mohamed Habeeb, ; C.I. Ernden vs State of Uttar Pradesh, AIR 1964 SC 575; and Lohana Kantilal vs State, AIR 1954 Saurashtra 12 1, referred to. (2) The words 'unless the contrary is proved ' which occur in this provision make it clear that the presumption has to be rebutted by 'proof ' and not by a bare explanation which is merely plausible. A fact is said to be proved when its existence is directly established or when upon the material before it the Court finds its existence to be so probable that a reasonable man would act on the supposition that it exists. Unless, there fore, the explanation is supported by proof, the presumption created by the provision cannot be said to ' be rebutted. [437H; 339A] State vs Mohamedubibeeb., ; C R. Erudernden v State of U.P., AIR 1954 SC 575 and Loahana Kantilal V.

The petitioner was an Under Secretary to the Government of India in the Ministry of Shipping and Transport and on May 21, 1974 accepted employment as Joint Manager in the Mogul Line Limited, a Government of india undertaking after obtaining release from government service. He was first allotted a service quarter. In 1975 the company purchased a spacious flat being flat No. 151 in Jolly Maker apartment III at 119 Cuffe Parade and the petitioner being the senior most executive was allotted the flat for his residence. The petitioner retired from the service of the company on or about September 30, 1984. Prior to that i.e. On September 26, 1984 he addressed a letter requesting the company to permit him to continue to live in the company 's premises during the period of his accumulated leave after his retirement and in accordance with the company rules, he was required to pay compensation for the use of the premises. After the expiry of the said period of six months, the company addressed a letters requesting the petitioner to vacate the flat stating that if he failed to do so, he would be liable to pay higher compensation as per the company"s rules. Since the petitioner failed to vacate, the Company initiated proceedings for his eviction under the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised occupants) Act, 1971. The Estate Officer by order dated December 2, 1985 directed the eviction of the petitioner. The Petitioner filed a suit in the Court of Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate 37th Court Esplanade, Bombay alleging that he was wrongfully withholding the flat in question which had been given to him for his own residence during the periods of his employment and thereby committed an offence punishable under section 630 of the Act. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the view expressed by the Single Judge following the earlier decisions of the High Court in Amritlal Chum vs Devi Devi Ranjan Ranjan Ranjan Jha, ; , that it refers only to the existing officers and employees of a company within the ambit of section 630 was limited to such property of the Company which was wrongfully obtained by an officer or employee of the companies. The High Court dismissed the special leave petition filed by the petitioner under Article 226 of the Constitution and held that the construction placed by the High court on the provisions contained in section 630(1) of the is the only construction possible construction possible. In the Special Leave Petition it was contended for the petitioner that the provision contained in Section 630 of tho Act is a penal provision and therefore must be subject to a strict construction and there is no room for intendment. It was further submitted that on a true construction, the scope and effect of the section was limited only to such properties of the Companies which was illegally obtained by the officer or employees of the firm and not to those whose employment has been terminated. The beneficent provision contained therein in Section 630(1), namely, where an officer and employee of a Company wrongfully withholds possession of property of a public company, or (b) having obtained such property during the course of his employ, to which he is not entitled; and that both clauses (a) and (b), are separated by the word 'or ' and therefore are clearly disjunctive.

The appellant was the founder of a Sansthan. The Sansthan was formed by the Maharaj who had movable property of the value of Rs. 19,164/ and immovable properties of the said Sansthan. In the year of account 18,164 61 were purchased from the temple by one Vithal Rukhamai. The appellant 's father died in 1952. The widow of the Sansthan filed a suit for declaration that the Sansthan was not a public trust. The trial court held that the deity was a private property and not a private trust. On appeal the District Judge reversed the decision holding that the appellant was a public Trust within the meaning of section 2(13) of the Act and restored the order of the Charity Commissioner. The High Court in revision set aside the order passed by the District judge and held that it was a Public Trust under section 29 of the , and therefore the appellant 'was not a trustee. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The High court was not right in giving due importance to the admission of the constituted attorney Ramkrishna Deshpande. [523 B] (2) The expression "public trust" is a very important piece of evidence to show that a public temple is a private one. The expression in the recital that "you are free as the full owner thereof" does not convert the gift which is expressly in favour of the deity or Sansthan into that in favour Of an individual as private property. [525 C D] (3) The definition of public trust contained in section 2 (13) and section 2 1(14) respectively of the Indian Trusts Act, 1882, shows that the property has always been treated as trust property even by the Officer saints and the Adhikaris or the disciples who succeeded one after the other were not owners but trustees of the property. The definition is very wide in its application to a public charitable trust. [500 D E] (4) In view of the fact that the temple was dedicated for the Darshan by the appellant, the endowment was a religious endowment within the scope of section 29 and the High Court was right in holding that it had no appearance of any impediment or restriction in the matter of continuous worship by the public extending over a long period. [511 C D; 512 A] (5) The position and purpose for which the trust was created, the consistent manner in which the property had been dealt with or managed by those in charge, the manner inwhich the property was dealt with, or managed, by those who were entitled to worship at the shrine of the temple, the nature of devolution of the properties, are all important elements in determination of the question whether a property is a public religious endowment. [506 B C] (6) The fact that a person has been appointed as manager of a temple does not make him a private or a body of persons interested. It is not always possible to have all the features of a public character without the least interference or restriction from the Temple authorities, to foster maintenance of the worship the accretion to the trust property by way of grants from the State of gifts from outsiders inconsistent with the private nature of the trust, the character of devolution being that of a religious trust. Therefore, in this case all the above tests are fulfilled. [605 C D]. (7) The properties in question were endowed for the worship of the public and the same had been managed by the saint. The fact of endowment was not such as to convert the gifts which was expressly in favor of the appellant.

The assessee was assessed to income tax for the years 1943 44 to 1947 1948 and 1951 52 by the Third Income tax Officer, C. 1 Ward, Bombay, at and for Rs. 40,178 4 0. The assessee not having paid up the assessed amount of tax the Income tax officer on the 10th April 1951 issued a warrant of arrest under section 13 of the Bombay City Land Revenue Act, 1876 requiring the assessee to appear before him in person on the 16th June 1955 and show cause why he should not be apprehended and confined to civil jail in satisfaction of the said certified demand. The sale proclamation was held on the 25th February 1955 fetching a price of Rs. 33,000 and it was confirmed on the 30th March 1955. On the 1st February 1954 the Additional Collector attached the goodwill and tenancy rights in the said premises by a warrant under section 46(2) of the Income Tax Act. The sales proclamation was issued on the 15th January 1955 and the sale proceeds not being sufficient to satisfy the assessed tax the Additional collector on the 7th June, 1955 issued a notice requiring the assesses to appear in person before him on the 8th July, 1955 and to show cause, why he, should not he apprehended and confine to civil prison in satisfaction Of the said demand. No payment having been made, the Additional Collec tor attached the good goodwill and the tenancy rights of the assessee by a warrants of attachment issued on 24th March 1954. The assessment order was confirmed by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. On further appeal by the assessee the High Court held that section 46 (2) which sanctions such discrimination is clearly violative of the equal protection clause of the Constitution and has, therefore, become void under article 13(1). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant: (i) that section 47(2), which sanctions a discrimination is not unconstitutional for the simple reason that the impugned law is based on a territorial classification having a reasonable nexus or correlation between that basis of classification and the object sought to be achieved by the Act, is founded on a comparison of the provisions of different laws adopted by different States for the recovery of land revenue; (ii) that in the matter of payment of public demands of the States the people of different States are not similarly situated and their own States have imposed on them such coercive processes as the circumstances and needs of each State require. Held:(i) The law impugned before this Court has only adopted for its own purpose, the same coercive process which was devised by the States for their own purposes which were closely akin or similar to the purpose of the Union. (ii)(a) It is a plausible argument to say that all the provisions Of all the State laws for recovery of arrears of land Revenue have been referentially incorporated in section 46.(2) at the time it was enacted to be treated as crystallised and to be applied by the Collectors, although the State law laws for the Recovery of arrears 'of land revenue may be materially altered by sub sequent amendment. (b) It cannot be said that all these provisions of all the States are, mutatis mutandis, to be read into section 46 of the Indian Income tax Act in extenso and it tells the Collectors of all other States to adopt the procedure prescribed by their own State laws as if the provisions prescribing that procedure were set out in that section.

The appellants are the trustees of a Port Trust Employees ' Union. The respondents to this appeal are the Trustees of the Port of Bombay. The dispute in the present case was whether the existing system of work of shore crew of the Prince 's and Victoria Docks under which each shift system consisted of 8 hours ' normal duty, 2 hours ' variable recess and 12 hours ' overtime needs any modification? The Tribunal held that the Union was not able to establish that the existing systems of work needed any modification. On appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants: (1) that section 13 fixes the number of hours constituting a normal working day for an adult can be so arranged that inclusive of intervals for rest it shall not spread over more than 12 hours on any day; and (2) that in some employments time for work depends on some 643 extraneous factors and hours of rest cannot always be fixed to, break up those hours. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (i) On a single day the number Of hours of work must not exceed 9 and together with the hours of ' rest the total period of work and rest should not go beyond 12 hours. It is wrong to contend that the period of 9 hours must always include intervals of rest. In a 12 hour shift, the nine hours of worked on any one day can be spread over 12 hours and the extra hours will necessarily be hours of part of the normal workingday which may also include one or more specified intervals. [637 B C] (ii) The scheme of the compels the inclusion of an hour of rest in a normal Working day is achieved by pres cribing that the hours Of work in a six day week shall not exceed 48, although on any particular day the hours are of rest, provided the period is specified beforehand, and the workman is neither called upon to work nor expected to work. Having thus distinguished between periods of work, and interval of rest it makes up their 9 hours which is 8 hours work and one hour interval for rest. They are, therefore, entitled to three hours ' wages overtime if required to work beyond the 9 hours on a day. [643 D E] (iii) The workmen compared the case of the Union that in the former there was 3 hours ' adolescent recess is in force at the Prince "s and James Docks work in different way and their case cannot be compared with that of the Flotilla Crew or the crew crew at the Alexandra Docks.

The appellant tenant was let out on June 25, 1976. The accommodation was for the first time assessed for house tax by Nagar Palika Ghaziabad with effect from October 1, 1976 and the accommodation was again for the second assessment year for house Tax by Nagar Mahapalika. The rent was for a period of 10 years. The suit was filed for eviction after termination of tenancy before the trial court and objection was raised that as the shop and the basement were separately let out the tenancy could not be terminated by a single notice that would be invalid. The trial court dismissed the suit. On appeal, the High Court set aside the decree and decreed the suit for ejectment on the ground that since the premises were let out in June 1976 but as the assessment was made on October 1. 1976, the provisions of the Act referred to above will not apply for 10 years from October l, 1976, and therefore, the suit could be decreed as the protection available under this Act will not be available to the tenant. In appeal by special leave, it was contended that since during the pendency of the proceedings in this Court 10 years had elapsed, the tenant would be entitled to the benefit of the provisions contained in section 20 of the East Punjab Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The right of a landlord to evict a tenant has been provided for in this Act under Section 20 and the language of Section 39 and 40 of the is clear that if the provisions Of this Act apply then no suit for eviction can be instituted except on the grounds specified in the sub sections of this section. [164G H] 2.

The respondent instituted a suit for ejectment of three persons, namely Abdul Rahim, Abdul Hamid and Abdul Gaffur from the property in suit (a parcel of land about 1 cottah 8 chittaks being part of premises No. 6 /1 Shibtola Lane), Calcutta. In the notice to quit served on the 7th May 1948, the first two defendants were described as thika tenants under the plaintiff and the third as a person who had purported to purchase the structures on the land and the tenancy right therein. The suit was contested only by the third defendant who filed a written statement in September 1948 contending that the suit was bad for non joinder of parties. The trial court decreed the suit but the appellate Court held that at the time when the appeal of the respondent was disposed of by the Subordinate Judge, the rights of the parties were governed by the Thika Tenancy Act of 1949 and the definition of thika tenant in that Act was not such as to afford any protection to the appellant. On a further appeal by the second defendant, the High Court held (i) that the appellant was not liable to ejectment in the absence of any grounds therefor in the notice dated June 18, 1948, as he was a thikatenant within the meaning of the Act as it was finally amended; and (ii) that even if no proceedings were pending in any court, it was open to the landlord to file a suit. In appeal by certificate to this Court, HELD: The benefit of section 28 was available only if the decree or order for recovery of possession had been made before the date of commencement of the 1949 Act but possession of such holding had not been recovered from him. If any pending suit or proceeding related to any matter in respect of which the Controller was competent to pass orders, the suit or proceedings would be transferred to the controller who would deal with it in accordance with the provisions of the West Bengal Thika Thika Amendment Ordinance 1952, i.e., 21st October 1952 and not in February 1949 i. e. the date when the commencement of that Act, it is not open to a landlord either to allege any of the grounds specified in section 3 or to prove the existence thereof at the hearing of the suit, he had to establish the existence of such a ground when the suit is heard. All that the section lays down is that ejectment could not be had unless the existence was one of the reasons was proved. [176 B C] Mahadeolal Kanodia vs Administrator General of West Bengal, ; , followed. Mahadeodolal Jodia vs administrator General ofWest Bengal, , approved.

The appellants were in the pay scale of Rs. 160 320 as against the pay scales of Rs,120 300 to Section Officers. In 1965 the State Government appointed a Pay Rationalisation Committee with wide ranging reference. The Committee recommended for them a pay scale slightly lower than that of Section Officers and Rs. 150 350 for Section Officers, but it suggested that ten posts of Bench Secretaries should be upgraded and placed in the Pay scale ofRs. 2000 1,000 as recommended by the Pay Commission. The appellants filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order dated July 2, 1976. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the State Govern ment had granted uniform pay scale to both the grades of Bench Secretary and Section Officers in view of their differential duties. It was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the Pay Reti tion Committee did not accept the claim of Bench Ministers for giving them pay scales equal to Section officers or Private Secretaries; (2) the creation of two Grades with different pay scales in the cadre of Bench Stenographers who were doing the same or similar work and responsibilities there cannot be two grades with different Pay scales. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Pay Commission refused to equate Bench Secretaries with Section Officers for equal work. It is found that the nature of duties and responsibilities of the two posts are quite different and more onerous than that Of Bench Secretaries. [306G] 2. The pay scale recommended by a Pay Commission was as follows: "Bench Secretary 26.38 Fifty two posts of Benches are in thepay scale of pay Rs.400750 and ten posts in the scale of RS.500 1,00000. The minimum pay scales is comparatively higher than the pay Scale of Upper Division Assistants though they were appointed through a competitive examination. The work of the Bench Secretary is of a great importance. [307A] 3. The Court Secretaries Grade I are selected among the lot of Bench Judges Grade II. When Benches Grade II acquire experience and also display more merit, they are appointed as Bench Secretaries Grade 1. When Bench Secretaries grade II acquired experience and even display more merits, they were appoint ed as Bench Secretary Grade I. [308B] 4. The rules thus make a proper classification for the purpose of entitlement to higher pay scale. The classification made under the Rules, therefore cannot be said to be violative of the right to have equal pay for equal Work.[307C D] 5. The principle of "equal pay for Equal work" has to be construed in the first place. Functions may be the same but the responsibilities make a difference. One cannot deny that often the difference is a matter of degree and that there is an element of value judgment by those who are charged with the administration in fixing the scales of pay and other conditions of service. So long as such value judgment emphasise that equal payfor equal work is a concomitant of Article 14 of the Constitution, but this principle naturally follows that equal Pay for equal duty will be a negation of that right. And said: "The same amount of physical work may entail different quality of work, some more sensitive. some requiring more tact, some less it varies from nature and culture of employment. If it has a rational nexus with the object to be sought for, as reiterated before a certain amount of value Judgment of the administrative authorities who are charge sheeted with fixing the payscales has to he left with them and it cannot be interfered with by the Court unless it is demonstrated that either it is irrational or based on no basis or arrived mala fide either in law or in fact. [309D E] 6. The State Government has granted uniform Pay scale scale of `Pay Rs. 1600 2950 to both these grades of Judges with effect from January 1, 1986.

The appellant company was incorporated under the , the entire share capital being owned by the Government of India. Powers were conferred on the Special Area Development Authority to impose property tax on lands and buildings within their jurisdiction. The procedure for imposition of taxes is contained in section 129 of the Municipalities Act and section 133 of the Municipal Corporation Act, 1956. By section 1(2) of that Act, the provisions inserted in the Municipalities (Amendment) Act 1976 were deemed to have come into force with effect from April 1, 1976. On June 24, 1976 respondent 1 made a further demand of Rs. 11 The appellant Company disputed its liability to pay the aforesaid amounts on the grounds, inter alia, that no tax was leviable on its property since the company was owned wholly by the government of India and that respondent I was estopped from levying the property tax by reason of the agreement of 1976. The first contention of the Attorney General was that respondent 1 could exercise only such powers to levy property tax as the Municipal Council or the Municipal council had under the Madhya Pradesh Municipalities Act, 1961 or the Madhya Bharat Municipalities Act. The High Court dismissed the writ petition filed by the appellant company. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that since the appellant companies were wholly owned by Government of india and that Respondent 1 was estopped by reason thereof, the property taxes imposed on them must be taken to have been incorporated in section 69(d) of the Act of 1973 and any subsequent change in those provisions by amendment of the two Acts cannot be availed of by respondent 1. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: (1) The object behind the declaration contained in Section 2 of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957 is not in any manner defeated by the legitimate exercise of taxing power under section 69 (d) or by the State Legislature. [16C] (2) The legislative field covered by Entry 23 of List II will pass on to Parliament by virtue of Entry 54, List I. But in order to 20 judge whether, on that account, the State legislature loses its competence to pass the Act, it is necessary to have regard to the object and purpose of that legislation and to the relevant provisions thereof, under which Special Area development Authorities are given the power to tax lands and building within their Jurisdiction. [17D] (3) The true effect behind the declarations contained in s 2 of Mines and Mineral (Regulation & Development)Act, 1957, is not the same thing as that of section 127A of the Madhya pradesh Municipalities Act which provides that property tax shall be paid primarily by the owner. It is true that on account of the declaration made by Parliament in respect of a declared industry and that the State Government had no competence to enact the impugned law by reason or Entry 52, List 1 read with Entry 24, List II.

The appellant was the lessee of a slate quarries in Venkatagiri. On January 10, 1942, an agreement was entered into between the Rajah of Venkatagiri and one Sri Balumuri Nageswara Rao whereby the Raja agreed to give annual leases in respect of certain slate quarry within his estate for five years in succession commencing from February 1942 if the lease were given continuously for 5 years, then the lessee would be entitled at the end of the fifth year to obtain a lease from the Rajah for a period of 20 years commencing from the termination of the sixth year. On December 10, 1947, the appellant applied to the Collector for confirmation of the lease granted by the Raja to him. The Board of Revenue passed an order on December 27, 1955 declaring that the lease to the appellant had been granted subsequent to July 1, 1945 and that as the lease was for a periods exceeding one year it was not enforceable against the Government according to the second proviso to section 20(1) of the Abolition Act. On appeal by the Board of revenue, the Board held that the lessee had been given notice before such termination and that the appellant 's lease was valid. The appellant then filed writ petition in the High Court praying for a writ of mandamus directing the State of Andhra Pradesh to forbear from terminating his leasehold right in the slate mines and from interfering with his possession and working of the slates and other ancillary reliefs. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the termination was bad as it did not give three months ' notice to the lessee or provide for any compensation as required by section 20 of the Act. Held, that on a true construction of the provisions of the Madras Estates Land (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948, which were passed under the Government of India Act, 1935, did offend section 299 of that Act and expressly save those Acts. The Abolition Act was one of the Acts included in the Ninth Schedule and was protected by article 31B. A. M.S. V.M. & Co. vs The State of Madras, ; , followed.
